articles.title_orig: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.content_orig:
North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member
Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.
The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.
He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.
Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.
Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.
The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.
Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
The 3km bridge opened in mid-October , 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.
The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June , his first trip there in seven years.
Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday , however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.title_zh: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.content_orig:
Power lines near the Gravelines Nuclear Power Station in Gravelines, France on Sept. 15
Recent weeks have brought red flag after red flag for investment in AI and the related data center boom. Bond yields soared for AI infrastructure giant CoreWeave, a sign that investors view the buildout as increasingly risky. And Meta’s reporting of negative free cash flow for the quarter to fund its infrastructure buildout while saying it might need to raise even more capital to fund its AI buildout not only hit its own stock but contributed to a price decline across the big tech companies.
These developments raised questions across Wall Street about whether too much is being spent too quickly on data center expansion. How questions over data center investment play out has big implications for how companies and investors approach the future of energy and, by extension, climate . A pullback in the pace of new data centers could ease pressure to build fossil generation, but it would also weaken the commercial case for clean energy technologies that need big, reliable buyers who are willing to pay a premium for power.
Most obviously, a dent in the AI buildout would translate directly into a slowdown in related electricity demand growth. In advanced economies like the U.S., data centers will account for 20% of that growth through 2030. By then, data centers are expected to account for 3% of global electricity demand, according to data from the International Energy Agency.
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
Some climate advocates may initially rejoice at slowing electricity demand. Even as renewable energy expands, grids around the world still rely on fossil fuels. In the U.S. in particular, AI demand has sparked a wave of building new natural gas infrastructure. In the short term, slowing demand would mean lower emissions from the existing system than today’s baseline assumptions and less investment in new natural gas infrastructure.
But a slowing data center build out leaves less mature technologies at risk. From advanced geothermal to new ways of producing nuclear power, big tech companies have been willing to pay more to lock in reliable power sources, thereby accelerating the market for these new efforts. Even unproven technologies like nuclear fusion have received a big financial boost from tech firms speculating that they might help solve their power challenges and give them a competitive leg up in the AI race. In a tighter financial environment with lower projected electricity demand, both the incentive and the financial capacity to make bold bets diminish.
To be clear, data centers are not the only source of growing electricity demand. New manufacturing continues to create the need for power. The need for air conditioning has ramped up in many emerging markets, particularly in the Global South, creating new grid pressures. And electric vehicles continue to take off in many markets outside the U.S.
Even as gas remains resilient, much of the power built to meet demand will come from clean sources, including and especially solar and battery storage. Solar is increasingly cost competitive. And this year’s spike in fuel prices—particularly natural gas—has made local power more appealing. But the companies behind growing sectors like air conditioning and EVs are less involved in local power systems and lack the capital to really shape them like the world’s wealthiest tech companies have. In short, clean energy will take a hit without the backing of big tech.
It’s too soon to tell whether, in the long run, this week’s AI infrastructure recalibration will be a blip in time or part of a much broader realignment. But it’s something that anyone invested in clean energy and climate should be watching closely.

articles.title_orig: How one man became the unsung hero of the internet during a cyber-security scramble
articles.title_zh: How one man became the unsung hero of the internet during a cyber-security scramble
articles.content_orig:
For more than 20 years, Ondřej Surý has been quietly helping to keep websites around the world running securely, largely in his spare time.
He voluntarily maintains software for two of the most popular versions of Linux, a free operating system similar to Windows, which are often used on web servers.
Typically, this involves keeping them up-to-date with the latest version of PHP, a programming language which underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
This week, he became very busy indeed.
With the help of AI, two major cyber-security flaws were identified in the programming language, leading the the PHP Foundation to release fixes.
But average folk may struggle to understand how to install these onto their systems - so Surý, for free, dropped everything to convert the fixes into packages, which can be easily installed without expertise.
"The feeling is like I am responsible for all these people and I can't fail them," he told BBC News.
The vulnerabilities in PHP sparked an international scramble to install security updates, amid fears that cyber criminals could exploit the gaps.
Surý is one of a small number of developers whose work helps make those updates available.
And while keeping the internet secure might sound like a full-time occupation, it isn't actually his day job.
He works as director of DNS engineering at Internet Systems Consortium, a US non-profit organisation.
But in his spare time, he has spent more than two decades voluntarily maintaining PHP software packages for the Linux versions Debian and Ubuntu.
He takes the source code released by the PHP project and turns it into packages which website operators can easily install on their servers.
When asked how it felt to be described as one of the people who helped "save the internet" this week as some online put it, his response was modest.
"It's kind of fulfilling because I sense my work has a purpose," he said.
"At the same time, I feel that not enough credit has been given to other people who has been part of this, like the PHP project people."
But he also acknowledged the weight that comes with his role.
Surý had been given advanced warning about the vulnerabilities by the PHP project, but when information about the weaknesses leaked online, the planned release was brought forward and things started ramping up.
"I got aware that this is quite severe and I don't have that much time to prepare the packaging of the PHP that I provide to people," he said.
Despite the urgency, he said he was confident that his experience and preparation would allow him to get the job done.
Other developers around the world were also working to ensure the patches could be distributed - highlighting just how much of the internet's essential infrastructure sometimes depends on dedicated developers.
Surý said this week had prompted an outpouring of support from people who relied on his software packages.
He revealed that he received more than $10,000 (£7,470) in donations in just a few days.
"This week is basically about a year's worth of the contributions that I got before," he said.
He said major technology companies should take more responsibility for supporting the open source software they depend upon.
"I think they should be more responsible," he said.
"If you just take and don't give back then it will backfire."
Surý has also been considering what would happen if he could no longer maintain the software packages himself.
He said colleagues at software company Freexian could take over, but they do not yet have the same accumulated experience.
"Yes, that's pretty much true," he said, when I asked him whether much of the responsibility ultimately rested with him.
But he is concerned that AI may be dramatically accelerating the discovery of security vulnerabilities, helping both cyber criminals and those trying to stop them.
"I think this is was the most severe incident in years, but I think that because of the AI capabilities are getting better in the cyber security, this might not be an isolated incident," he said.
"And people should be prepared to act this quickly more often because incidents like this might happen in the future - in the near future."

articles.title_orig: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.title_zh: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.content_orig:
Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.
The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.
The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.
This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.
As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.
Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.
National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.
With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.
To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.
From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.
For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.
But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.
Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.
When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.
The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."
It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.
Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."
Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.
The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.
This is a row that is playing out in the election.
There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.
Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.
Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.
All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.
A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.

articles.title_orig: Arrests in Barcelona after 'anti-system' rioters loot shops, set fires
articles.title_zh: Arrests in Barcelona after 'anti-system' rioters loot shops, set fires
articles.content_orig:
A total of 100 people were arrested in Barcelona on Saturday evening after hooded demonstrators who participated in an anti-establishment rally looted shops and set fire to street furniture around the city's central Plaza de Catalunya.
Núria Parlon, the interior minister for the Spanish region of Catalonia , said around 25% of those arrested were minors. More than 30 fires were set and 14 stores vandalized or looted in a part of town popular with tourists and weekend shoppers, she added.
Demonstrators were called in social media posts to a movement "against the system." The posts also used the slogan "Institut Indignats," a translation of the movement "Lyceés Indignés," which was used to rally students who have protested in France in recent weeks. In English, the phrase translates as "Indignant High School Student."
Social media videos show people trapped inside shops, including department store El Corte Inglés, after shutters were lowered to prevent looting . Other posts showed hooded demonstrators dressed in black kicking in shop windows and making off with goods, in some cases encouraged by online viewers.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said acts of vandalism in the city "will not go unpunished," including legal consequences for the guardians of any minors involved.

articles.title_orig: Six Flags Will Add Seatbelts to Some Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
articles.title_zh: Six Flags Will Add Seatbelts to Some Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags will add seat belts to Goliath and other roller coasters with similar restraints following the death of a man who fell from the ride at Six Flags Over Georgia earlier this month.
The company’s CEO said in a statement Friday that Goliath remains closed pending safety reviews and clearances following the death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old Atlanta resident and “cherished member” of a public charter school, who fell from the coaster on October 12 . Several other parkgoers were injured, including four minors, police said.
In a statement addressed to guests and passholders, Six Flags President and CEO John Reilly said the company is reinforcing safety precautions across its parks, including installing seat belts on the Goliath, and has engaged independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across its attractions.
Goliath, a 3.5-minute ride reaching 70 mph and a height of 200 feet, features a waist restraint but does not have an over-the-shoulder harness . The addition of seat belts marks a significant change to the ride’s restraint system as investigators continue to examine what happened.
“Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” Reilly said, adding that the company is committed to evaluating the findings and taking appropriate action.
“Safety also depends on the dedicated teams who operate and maintain our attractions every day. Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience, with additional instruction and evaluation provided as necessary,” he continued.
Goliath and eight other rides at five additional Six Flags parks remain temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution, according to the company. Six Flags said its parks remain open, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across its properties.
Preliminary information gathered at the scene from witnesses and employees indicated Kariem had been ejected from the ride, the Cobb County Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit said. He struck other riders before falling beneath the roller coaster, where he was found “unresponsive and not breathing,” police said in a statement.
One witness, CiCi Nelson , told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when a cart pulled up with an empty seat and other riders in hysterics.
She said the safety bar on the empty seat appeared loose, and another young passenger appeared to be covered in blood and injured. Emergency personnel quickly arrived, and she and others were asked to evacuate the area.
The announcement of the new seat belt installations follows the reopening of Six Flags Over Georgia last Friday, when visitors returned for the park’s annual Halloween Fright Fest events. Goliath remained closed as families entered the park, and officials offered no new findings about the fatal incident.
What we know about the fatal roller coaster incident at Six Flags Over Georgia
Georgia authorities are investigating the death, reviewing evidence, equipment and documentation to determine whether state safety requirements were followed, according to a statement last week from Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King. Cobb County police are assisting state and park officials.
CNN has reached out to Cobb County, Cobb County Police and the Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner for an update on the investigation into Kariem’s death and comment on Six Flags’ plans to add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters.
As the investigation remains underway, CNN analysis has revealed alleged maintenance issues and guest injuries at several Six Flags parks.
CNN’s review of safety records from 2016 through 2026 found that Goliath appeared to have passed annual state safety inspections. The coaster’s most recent inspection, on March 16, reported no violations, deficiencies, citations or red tags, according to King. A separate inspection report earlier this year noted that bushings, which are components that help reduce vibration, on the coaster needed replacement, according to CNN affiliate WSB.
“I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “As CEO of Six Flags, I take that responsibility personally.”
CNN’s Isa Mudannayake, Karina Tsui, Isabel Rosales, and Julianna Bragg contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: French protests: Almost 1,000 arrested, Laurent Nuñez says, as clashes erupt
articles.title_zh: French protests: Almost 1,000 arrested, Laurent Nuñez says, as clashes erupt
articles.content_orig:
This live page is now closed, but you can read more in our news story
Almost 1,000 people have been arrested during protests across France, the interior minister says, as clashes erupt after a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations
In Porte de Vincennes, Paris, protesters threw objects towards the police, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux
Police fired tear gas in cities including Lyon and Nantes as hundreds of thousands took to the streets across France - 110,000 protesters marched in Paris alone, police say
Tear gas filled my eyes as protest turned ugly, writes our reporter in Paris , showing how violent standoffs mark the end of these bouts of unrest
Today's marches follow last weekend's riots and looting that saw more than 2,700 arrested across France - why are people protesting?
Elsewhere in Europe, protests have also been taking place today in Brussels, Rome and Milan
Edited by Matt Spivey and Charlotte Hadfield, with Nick Beake and Mark Lowen in Paris
Jacob Phillips Live reporter
Protesters take cover behind a plywood board as French riot police use a water canon in Paris
French police have fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse protesters as clashes broke out following a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations across France.
Almost 1,000 people have been arrested, according to officials, as an estimated 410,000 people rallied across the country. The unions put the number at about 800,000.
In Paris, our reporterâs eyes were filled with tear gas as a protest turned ugly in the French capital, with objects thrown towards police.
In Marseille, barricades and rubbish bins were set alight, while protesters ripped boards from a shop to build a street barricade in Bordeaux.
Meanwhile in southeastern city of Grenoble, hundreds of masked individuals carried out acts of vandalism and attacked police âwith mortars and projectilesâ, according to officials.
Officials have so far managed to avoid a repeat of last weekend's rioting and looting, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history. More than 2,700 people were arrested following the mass disorder on 17 October.
We are ending our live coverage now, but you can read more about the French protests here .
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.
A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as demonstrators were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.
Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.
Protesters face police during the demonstrations in Marseille
The mayor of Marseille says several groups attempted to loot different parts of the city on Saturday.
BenoÃ®t Payan asks people in Marseille to "remain cautious" and to work with police and the emergency services.
French media reports 51 people were arrested in the city including 20 adults, citing the region's prefecture.
Sarah Rainsford Southern Europe correspondent, in Milan
A major security operation including the deployment of 100s of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering for most of the day in Milan .
It was part of the governmentâs zero tolerance response after violent scenes in the city last week when some demonstrators set fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
There were protests today elsewhere in Italy , including skirmishes with police in Bologna , where water cannons were used, and Turin where protesters also burned a picture of the prime minister.
But early this afternoon a man described as the 'brains' behind the 17 October Movement (M1710) which had called today's protests was identified and taken in for questioning by police.
The mysterious movement had promised to post details on social media of where to gather in each city - in order to avoid the police - but its social media accounts were never updated.
Here in Milan , that left would-be protesters lost for what to do, or where to go, and easily outnumbered and outmanoeuvred by police and paratroopers.
We saw groups - mostly teenagers - being stopped and searched on a massive scale, with police checking their bags and documents.
Later in the evening, a crowd of demonstrators marched peacefully through the city, ending outside the Polytechnic University.

U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.
A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.
The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.
Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June.
Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.
The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.
Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

articles.title_orig: Secret Russian Funding Revealed in Trump-Putin Energy Scheme
articles.title_zh: Secret Russian Funding Revealed in Trump-Putin Energy Scheme
articles.content_orig:
A multibillion-dollar project to tap into natural gas in Alaska pursued by the Trump administration has been revealed to have secretly received funding from a sanctioned Russian company, according to a report.
Polar LNG, an American energy startup, is seeking to buy Russian technology to extract natural gas from Alaska's North Slope and ship it to allies abroad, portraying the project as a decidedly American undertaking.
But Joel Riddle, who resigned as the company's chief executive last month, told The New York Times that he was misled about the source of the company's funding. He said he had been made to believe that the money came from a firm in the United Arab Emirates, when at least some of it actually came from Novatek, one of Russia's biggest energy companies that is under partial U.S. sanctions.
"It's not only unlawful, but it's not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope," Riddle told the Times.
Yet President Donald Trump's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the project with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin during negotiations last month for a deal to end his war on Ukraine, people familiar with the talks told the Times.
The U.S. sanctions on Novatek mean the Treasury Department would need to approve the use of its equipment in Alaska, and a sanctions bill passed by Congress named after late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina specifically targets Novatek over the company's ties to Putin. Trump waived the law's sanctions last week.
Witkoff and Kushner's willingness to entertain such a deal is a striking example of how Trump and his inner circle have mixed the business of ending a war with the business of making deals, rather than focusing solely on putting an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
In the latest twist, Novatek told the Times on Friday that it was moving to acquire "minority shareholder" status in the Polar LNG project, potentially giving a sanctioned Russian energy giant a stake in U.S. gas production.
But even a memo prepared for Polar LNG by outside law firm Baker Botts warned that perceived ties to Novatek could jeopardize licenses and other regulatory approvals, according to the Times. The memo also said federal officials had already expressed concern that one of Polar LNG's investors had links to Novatek and might be acting on the Russian company's behalf.
Ilya Zaslavskiy, a gas industry consultant who studies Russian sanctions and energy issues in Washington, slammed Polar LNG's dealings with Novatek and argued that it should have no place in negotiations over ending the war.
"Any approach by Novatek to transfer technology should be seen as a Kremlin attempt to co-opt U.S. policymakers in order to undermine U.S. foreign policy toward Ukraine and our allies," Zaslavskiy told the Times.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: He Bought a Mansion for $155M, Had It Torn Down
articles.title_zh: He Bought a Mansion for $155M, Had It Torn Down
articles.content_orig:
For America’s billionaires, even a $100 million mansion can be a teardown.
The ultrawealthy are snapping up lavish estates — only to send in the bulldozers, treating perfectly good homes as little more than obstacles standing between them and their dream properties.
In March 2023, cosmetics billionaire William Lauder, an heir to the Estée Lauder fortune, shelled out a staggering $155 million for the late conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh’s sprawling estate in Palm Beach — a roughly 24,000-square-foot oceanfront mansion complete with a Versailles-inspired salon and an ornate library modeled after one at the Biltmore Estate.
Four months later, the house was rubble.
The extraordinary demolition is among the most extreme examples of a luxury real estate trend sweeping wealthy enclaves across the country, according to the Wall Street Journal .
In exclusive enclaves such as Palm Beach, where prime oceanfront land is increasingly scarce, even lavish, relatively modern mansions are being treated as disposable.
The real prize isn’t the house — it’s the irreplaceable piece of land beneath it.
Lauder had already razed two other oceanfront homes elsewhere in Palm Beach, including one that was just six years old.
He later sold the cleared lots for close to $200 million in 2025 to a buyer with ties to Microsoft .
The properties became part of a larger, multimillion-dollar land assemblage that could eventually rank among Palm Beach’s priciest private estates.
WeatherTech founder David MacNeil has also made a habit of buying and demolishing multimillion-dollar properties in nearby Manalapan.
MacNeil paid $55.5 million for a partially completed mansion in Manalapan in 2025, after purchasing the neighboring property for $38.5 million the year before.
He demolished both homes, combining the properties into a 3.5-acre oceanfront lot that he listed for $125 million before selling it for $105 million earlier this year.
In another deal, MacNeil paid $36 million in July for a roughly 9,000-square-foot home built around 2004, directly adjacent to his primary residence.
That house also met the wrecking ball.
MacNeil plans to replace it with a fitness center and green space, telling the Journal the existing property was outdated and would have required an estimated $10 million in renovations.
And he has teamed up with another billionaire neighbor to secure even more land.
In June, MacNeil and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison struck deals totaling $67 million to split a 4-acre waterfront parcel between their neighboring Manalapan estates.
The land had previously been earmarked for a proposed $285 million megamansion , with plans calling for a roughly 50,000-square-foot residence packed with luxury amenities.
The teardown craze is also reshaping how luxury properties are marketed.
A Palm Beach oceanfront compound belonging to the late developer Murray Goodman and his wife, Joanie, recently hit the market for $185 million.
Despite being in good condition, the roughly 2-acre estate — complete with pink-hued buildings, a tennis court and 250 feet of direct ocean frontage — is widely expected to be demolished by its next owner, local agents told the Journal.
Meanwhile, Ellison has relisted his seven-bedroom North Palm Beach estate for $165 million.
Although the Tuscan-style mansion, built in the 1990s, remains in good condition, listing agents James Kenny and Paul Kaneb of K2 Realty told the Journal they are marketing it as a potential redevelopment opportunity.
The obsession with starting from scratch isn’t limited to Palm Beach.
In Houston’s affluent Bunker Hill Village, more than 15% of home listings contain terms associated with teardowns, such as “rebuild” or “land value,” according to Redfin data cited by the Journal.
In Pimmit Hills, Virginia, a postwar neighborhood in Fairfax County, the share is 6.67%.
And the appetite for fresh construction is raising questions about the environmental cost of treating luxury homes as disposable.
William Paddock of environmental consulting firm WAP Sustainability told the Journal that replacing a 10,000-square-foot house with a 30,000-square-foot mansion would carry a carbon footprint comparable to powering roughly 250 average US homes for a year.
South Florida contractor Robert Burrage told the Journal that only about 25% of materials from homes demolished by his firm end up in landfills, with appliances and cabinetry donated and materials such as concrete and metal sorted for reuse.

articles.title_orig: ‘In three days, we can start writing a different story’: Masses at anti-gov’t rally demand Oct. 7 inquiry
articles.title_zh: ‘In three days, we can start writing a different story’: Masses at anti-gov’t rally demand Oct. 7 inquiry
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Israelis are protesting against the government and calling for an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks .
Demonstrators rallied in the public plaza known as Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday, three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
Elsewhere in Israel, protesters were also gathering for antigovernment demonstrations, reported Haaretz newspaper.
Taking part were leading figures from opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main centre-right rival.
In Tel Aviv, Eisenkot was greeted by chants of “Who’s coming? The next prime minister”, according to The Times of Israel. The leader of the Democrats, Yair Golan, was also at the rally.
“Masses, masses of masses, flowing in the ‘Democrats’ march from Rabin Square to the Hostages Square – for change, for hope, for r-e-v-o-l-u-t-i-o-n. What energy. This time it’s ours completely!”, Israeli citizen and lawyer Dan Adin posted on X.
Polls ahead of Tuesday’s election suggest a tight race, with Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, in power since late 2022, neck and neck with Eisenkot’s. Neither bloc is currently projected to obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s parliament.
The election could be pivotal in determining whether Israel launches another round of strikes on Iran. Eisenkot is believed to be less inclined to resume military action against Tehran if he becomes Israel’s next prime minister.
However, on most other foreign policy issues, leading Israeli parties and politicians remain united, including in their opposition to the creation of an independent Palestinian state.
Ahead of the protest, the October Council alerted law enforcement to possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
“We have sent an urgent letter to the Police Commissioner following alerts about attempts by entities linked to the coalition to disrupt tonight’s rally,” it wrote on X.
The October Council aims to hold Israeli officials deemed responsible for the October 7 attacks to account and deliver justice for affected families.
Netanyahu’s coalition government, however, has refused demands to establish an independent commission of inquiry. Instead, it has offered to set up a “political” commission. Half of the commission’s members would be appointed by the government, while the remainder would be appointed by opposition legislators.
Opposition leaders have said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

articles.title_orig: Protests spread from Paris to other capital cities across Europe
articles.title_zh: Protests spread from Paris to other capital cities across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Protests over a range of issues have taken place in cities across Europe, from Milan and Madrid to Lisbon and Tirana. Demonstrators are taking to the streets over pensions, housing, education, corruption and opposition to war, reflecting a diverse mix of grievances across the continent.
Despite precautions, bans and heavy policing the protests led to violent clashes in several cities in France - around 2,400 people have been arrested, while nearly 1000 members of the security forces were injured, as well 100 protesters and residents in Paris alone.
Thousands of people rallied for a fresh anti-government protest in the Albanian capital Tirana on Saturday, with police firing tear gas to disperse the crowd. In the latest of several clashes between police and protesters since mid-October, government buildings were attacked and dozens of demonstrators were detained. Authorities said that more than 300 protestors and police have been injured.
Thousands took to the streets in Milan, Rome, Turin, Naples, Bologna and Florence with protester throwing bottles, stones and firecrackers.
Italian police said in a statement they had carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement added.
In Madrid the protesters' key demands include linking pension increases to actual inflation, raising the minimum pension to match the minimum wage, closing the gender pension gap and protecting the public pension system from privatisation.
In Portugal affordable housing is the main demand

A man in Germany was arrested on suspicion of arson this week after he allegedly set fire to a mountain retreat built for Adolf Hitler.
The fire broke out at the Eagle’s Nest in the Bavarian Alps on Friday evening, and firefighters battled the flames against strong winds.
The 33-year-old suspect is a German citizen who showed signs of mental illness and was taken to a psychiatric facility, authorities said.

But they aren’t ruling out a political motive for the arson due to its notorious history.
He was seen heading down the mountain on a motorcycle.
The Kehlsteinhaus, as it’s called in Germany, is more than 6,000 feet above sea level and accessible by an elevator during the day for tourists.
The building has operated as a seasonal restaurant and tourist attraction since 1952, and has an exhibit on its history .

He did frequent his Berghof residence in the same area, which was blown up after the war.
"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters at Eagle’s Nest. "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

He added: "It is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

articles.title_orig: Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear
articles.title_zh: Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear
articles.content_orig:
Heidi Levine, the Washington Post journalist brutally attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank last week, said the terrifying ordeal has only strengthened her resolve to continue covering the plight of Palestinians.
“What hurts me the most is I can now really understand what others have gone through, what Palestinian women, children, men have gone through,” she told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday from Israel, where she’s recovering after being released from hospital the day before.
“I’m an American, I work for the Washington Post, my story is getting a lot of attention around the world, everyone wants to talk to me – but I can’t imagine what it’s like for all the victims that have gone through the same ordeal and are living with the threat of this violence on a daily basis,” she added.
“It actually has strengthened my commitment to continue working to try to make a difference.”
Levine, a veteran photojournalist known for her work in the Middle East, was covering the annual olive harvest in the West Bank when she, a group of Palestinians, and other journalists came under attack. Violence in the West Bank has surged in recent years as settlements have expanded, often backed by Israeli forces; attacks on farmers and communities who rely on the olive harvest for their livelihoods now come on a daily basis.
Initially, Levine said, the harvest began as planned. But then, peering through her telephoto camera lens, she noticed people gathering at a nearby hilltop. They seemed young, some wearing black masks; she could see religious garments and headwear like kippah and tzitzit that she said clearly identified them as Israeli settlers.
Washington Post journalist hospitalized after Israeli settler attack on Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
Their numbers slowly grew to reach several dozen. They began lighting the olive trees on fire and moving closer. “Then all of a sudden, chaos broke out,” she said.
“There was tear gas, there was gunfire. From what I understand, a man was shot; a Palestinian man was shot in the leg, and the settlers charged forward,” she said.
“I was thrown to the ground … They just kept kicking me and hitting me with sticks, and it just kept going on and on. And then I actually thought, okay, maybe I’ll just play dead and pretend I’m dead, and they’ll stop and they’ll leave me alone.”
Instead, her attackers started ripping her gear off her body – her camera bag, her lenses, her pouch containing her American passport, credit cards, documents and other items.
Then they hauled her to her feet, in a moment that has sparked controversy and debate in the week since videos of her attack emerged. In a statement after the attack, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.”
This, Levine says, was false.
“No, they only stood me up because they couldn’t manage to get everything off my shoulders to rob me, including ripping off my gold necklace that my daughter gave me for my birthday,” she said.
The attack finally halted when journalist Jasper Nathaniel and several others came to Levine’s aid – but the danger wasn’t over. Video footage from that moment shows her rescuers holding her up and trying to escape from the attackers, who continue to throw rocks as they give chase.
“Run, run!” Levine’s rescuers can be heard shouting in a panic.
“I can’t,” she responds weakly. They urge her again: “You have to, come on!”
Speaking to Tapper on Thursday, she described it as “this biblical battle where the Palestinian men, a group of men went in front of me to protect us, me and my rescuers from being attacked again.” Without the Palestinians’ intervention, the whole group “would have been in the same situation as me.”
Even with a flak jacket and helmet on, Levine sustained serious injuries, with a broken rib, a broken vertebra, and a severe finger injury that required surgery, said Nathaniel last week after visiting her in the hospital. When she spoke to CNN, her hand was still heavily bandaged.
Her attack was widely condemned by foreign press, the White House, and some Israeli leaders including President Isaac Herzog. Netanyahu, however, tried to cast doubt on Levine’s attack and said that “serious questions remain.”
Just one day after Levine’s assault, settlers attacked a group of European diplomats visiting the Palestinian Christian town of Taybeh, prompting further outcry from the international community.
On Monday, Israeli police arrested at least 10 suspects for both attacks.
But many Palestinian victims of similar attacks never see justice. Since the olive harvest began on September 27, Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented more than 530 incidents of “settler and soldier violence” – which, beyond outright attacks, also includes the looting of crops and livestock, and destruction of olive trees.
More than a quarter of the violence “occurs in solders’ presence and under their protection,” said Yesh Din.
There has been a dramatic expansion of illegal settler outposts across the West Bank since Netanyahu’s government formed in December 2022 – with more than a third approved by the government. With that expansion, settler violence has also spread into parts of the West Bank that had previously seen little or none.
When asked if she blames Netanyahu and other far-right Israeli leaders like national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for her attack, Levine laughed humorlessly.
“Well, you hear their rhetoric, right? You hear their speeches. I’ve documented their visits in the West Bank, so I think the answer is pretty obvious,” she said, warning that things will only worsen, and that authorities “don’t even know how to handle it.”
“This has been going on for over four decades that I have been covering this region, but I’ve never seen this situation in the West Bank or the situation in Israel at the level that it is today.”

articles.title_orig: Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites; attacks reported in Aden
articles.title_zh: Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites; attacks reported in Aden
articles.content_orig:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports , killing at least 20 people.
The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday.
But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen.
"No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?
Saudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable.
Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf —   all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.
To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis —   along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.
To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes.
"Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent.
"There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area."
"If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.
Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.
The ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."
"Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.
Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors , while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit .
"If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"
Saudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data , but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.
Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones .
These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say.
They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News.
The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.
The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack."
"This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."
One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds .
Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on."
The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training.
Another issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.
Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean.
"You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said.
"If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."
Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.
The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5 . Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces .

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Israelis rally against Netanyahu gov’t days before election
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Israelis rally against Netanyahu gov’t days before election
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Israelis are protesting against the government and calling for an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks .
Demonstrators rallied in the public plaza known as Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday, three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
Elsewhere in Israel, protesters were also gathering for antigovernment demonstrations, reported Haaretz newspaper.
Taking part were leading figures from opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main centre-right rival.
In Tel Aviv, Eisenkot was greeted by chants of “Who’s coming? The next prime minister”, according to The Times of Israel. The leader of the Democrats, Yair Golan, was also at the rally.
“Masses, masses of masses, flowing in the ‘Democrats’ march from Rabin Square to the Hostages Square – for change, for hope, for r-e-v-o-l-u-t-i-o-n. What energy. This time it’s ours completely!”, Israeli citizen and lawyer Dan Adin posted on X.
Polls ahead of Tuesday’s election suggest a tight race, with Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, in power since late 2022, neck and neck with Eisenkot’s. Neither bloc is currently projected to obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s parliament.
The election could be pivotal in determining whether Israel launches another round of strikes on Iran. Eisenkot is believed to be less inclined to resume military action against Tehran if he becomes Israel’s next prime minister.
However, on most other foreign policy issues, leading Israeli parties and politicians remain united, including in their opposition to the creation of an independent Palestinian state.
Ahead of the protest, the October Council alerted law enforcement to possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
“We have sent an urgent letter to the Police Commissioner following alerts about attempts by entities linked to the coalition to disrupt tonight’s rally,” it wrote on X.
The October Council aims to hold Israeli officials deemed responsible for the October 7 attacks to account and deliver justice for affected families.
Netanyahu’s coalition government, however, has refused demands to establish an independent commission of inquiry. Instead, it has offered to set up a “political” commission. Half of the commission’s members would be appointed by the government, while the remainder would be appointed by opposition legislators.
Opposition leaders have said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

articles.title_orig: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.title_zh: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.content_orig:

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.
Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .
The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.
The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.
Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.
At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.
Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year,  Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. articles.title_orig: Verizon Apologizes for iPhone Duo Pre-Order Delays, Giving Customers $100 Gift Card
articles.title_zh: Verizon Apologizes for iPhone Duo Pre-Order Delays, Giving Customers $100 Gift Card
articles.content_orig:
Verizon has apologized to customers who pre-ordered the iPhone Duo through the carrier but have since been informed that their delivery is delayed.
In an email sent to affected customers, Verizon said an "unexpected shipping delay" means that iPhone Duo deliveries to some customers will "take a little longer." To make up for the inconvenience, Verizon is offering affected customers a $100 Verizon gift card that can be used online or in-store toward bill payments or merchandise.
"We owe you an apology," said Verizon. "We appreciate your patience and the opportunity to make this right," the company added.
Verizon said customers will receive an email about the $100 gift card next week, and it assured that it is working to fulfill orders as soon as it can.
"Your order is secure, your place in line hasn't changed, and our team is actively tracking your shipment to get it to you as quickly as possible," said Verizon.
MacRumors reader Ryan showed us that he pre-ordered an iPhone Duo from Verizon when pre-orders began on Friday, October 16. Verizon initially quoted him a Friday, October 23 delivery date, meaning he would have received the device on its launch day, but his estimated delivery date has since been revised to Saturday, November 7.
There are many similar examples of Verizon customers with delayed pre-orders across the MacRumors Forums , Reddit , and other social media platforms, with many revised delivery dates now falling in the October 31 to November 14 window.
Some customers who pre-ordered an iPhone Duo through Verizon did receive the device on October 23, so not everyone is impacted.
Last week, Apple said pre-order demand for the iPhone Duo was " nothing short of extraordinary ," with estimated delivery dates on its own online store pushing into late January for new orders. Some lucky customers managed to secure an iPhone Duo on a walk-in basis yesterday, while in-store pickup reservations resumed with little to no availability .
Leading up to the iPhone Duo launch, there were a few reports mentioning that there would be supply constraints due to alleged manufacturing challenges . In any case, getting the device early is proving to be a challenge for some.
In the meantime, Verizon said affected customers can check their iPhone Duo order status on the My Orders page via the My Verizon website or app.

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo Fails JerryRigEverything's Dusty Durability Test
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo Fails JerryRigEverything's Dusty Durability Test
articles.content_orig:
Apple's iPhone Duo has failed JerryRigEverything's latest durability test . Despite its IP68 dust-resistance rating, dust entered the hinge through several ingress points, overwhelming the magnets that hold the phone shut. The bend test then left a permanent green line across the inner display, before the screen became unresponsive.
The outer screen with Ceramic Shield 2 scratched at level 7 on the Mohs scale, but the inner screen only managed level 2, although credit was given for its matte nano-texture coating making marks "magically disappear." Alas, it wasn't enough to earn a pass. "I've been testing these folding phones since the first generation seven years ago – most do survive," said Nelson. "The iPhone Duo did not." Watch his full video here .

articles.title_orig: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.title_zh: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.content_orig:
Almost the entire management team of the US$25 billion US gas project Polar Train LNG has left the company following allegations of undisclosed financing and control by Russia's Novatek.
Details : The Financial Times reported that the company's former chief executive, Joel Riddle, raised concerns about potential violations of US sanctions.
Polar Train LNG is developing a gas export terminal in northern Alaska. The project was launched in March with a plan to use a partially constructed Novatek terminal and relocate it to Alaska. The company applied to the US Treasury Department for permission to negotiate with the Russian group but has yet to receive approval.
Riddle said he discovered that Novatek was already financing the project and directing its operations before the necessary approvals had been obtained. He resigned in September, after which chief financial officer Dan Chandra and other executives also left the company.
"I resigned as chief executive of Polar LNG because I felt uncomfortable that the Russian company Novatek was financing and ultimately controlling the strategic direction of the company," said Riddle.
He initially believed that the funding was being provided by Gentry Beach, an investor with ties to Donald Trump's family, and Abu Dhabi-based company Tech Wave. Riddle said he later discovered that Beach had not invested in the project and was neither a shareholder nor an executive.
The FT also reviewed WhatsApp messages in which Novatek board member Denis Solovyov discussed financing the project and sought to expedite the transfer of funds to Polar Train LNG.
Polar LNG said Riddle had been dismissed, described him as a "disgruntled employee" and stressed that it was developing the project in compliance with US law.
Novatek said it had agreed to grant Tech Wave the right to use its technology in Alaska and had signed a memorandum with Polar Train in April, when Riddle was still running the company.
According to people who spoke to the FT, the project had featured in talks between Washington and Moscow over business deals that could help bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. The discussions included a potential exchange under which Novatek would provide its expertise for the construction of the Alaska terminal in return for sanctions being lifted on Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s Starlink speeds restored after week of frontline disruption
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s Starlink speeds restored after week of frontline disruption
articles.content_orig:
Questions persist about who ordered the interruptions to the satellite internet system that Kyiv’s forces rely on to counter Russian attacks
Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.
“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said on social media, adding that restoration began overnight and was sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.
