articles.title_orig: UK police says letter with claims against Meghan's father was not shared with other law enforcement
articles.title_zh: UK police says letter with claims against Meghan's father was not shared with other law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she is "deeply distressed" by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation over claims he possessed images containing child sexual abuse in his home.
The images were reportedly found in his home in the Philippines after he returned to the U.S. in May, Philippine officials said.
Thomas Markle denied the allegations, calling them "sick lies" and "the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."
London's Metropolitan Police confirmed Saturday that it received a letter in January 2019 containing "a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," the BBC reported . The letter was sent to the force's protection command because of concerns about the duchess's security.
The Met said it passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex "for their awareness," but did not share the details with other law enforcement agencies. The force said it is reviewing how it handled the matter and considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, the police watchdog.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan Markle said that she is "deeply distressed" by the news, and that she was first made aware of the claims by the Met Police in 2018.
"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan's statement said. "In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
"I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."
Meghan had said the letter was sent in 2018. A spokesman for the duchess said Saturday that "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time."
Authorities in the Philippines are also investigating. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said national police had secured Markle's computer for a forensic examination, the BBC reported.
The allegations, reported by Mail Online , said Thomas Markle is under investigation after being reported by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
In a statement to Mail Online , the elder Markle said: "I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."
He added: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom [Markle] is trying to destroy me with these lies."
Yahoo has contacted the Met Office and authorities in the U.S. and the Philippines for comment.

articles.title_orig: Jared Kushner’s Lawyer Puts Vanity Fair on Notice Over ‘False’ Claims
articles.title_zh: Jared Kushner’s Lawyer Puts Vanity Fair on Notice Over ‘False’ Claims
articles.content_orig:
Jared Kushner ’s attorney says his legal team has formally put Vanity Fair and its parent company, Condé Nast, on notice over allegations about President Donald Trump ’s son-in-law that the lawyer characterized as “false and defamatory.”
The dispute centers on an excerpt from investigative journalist Matthew Cole’s forthcoming book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East .
The Vanity Fair excerpt alleges that Kushner had access to foreign accounts involving large sums of money during Trump ’s first term.
Kushner has categorically denied the allegations.
Newsweek reached out to Vanity Fair and Cole's representation by email for comment Saturday.
Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and served as a senior White House adviser during Trump’s first administration, from 2017 to 2021.
The allegations concern purported financial arrangements involving countries in the Middle East. According to Cole’s account, Dutch investigators obtained information from Kushner’s compromised phone and uncovered purported financial arrangements involving Middle Eastern governments.
Kushner denies the alleged events occurred.
Cole further alleges that Saudi and Emirati officials arranged for at least $2 billion to be placed in accounts that Kushner could access. The author also alleges that approximately $750 million was transferred into a UAE -linked account on which Kushner was a signatory. Kushner disputes the allegations, and TheWrap said it had not independently verified them.
President Donald Trump has also rejected the report , calling it “a totally false story.”
Kushner has remained involved in U.S. foreign policy after serving as a senior adviser during Donald Trump’s first administration, particularly on Middle East diplomacy. He joined U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in indirect negotiations with Iran in February 2026, talks mediated by Oman that its foreign minister said produced “significant progress.”
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) has accused Kushner of not being properly vetted for the role as one of Trump's top foreign policy representatives.
Kushner was set to travel with Vice President JD Vance and Witkoff in April to Pakistan for talks amid efforts to sustain a U.S.-Iran ceasefire.
In a letter, Kushner’s lawyers disputed the allegations and said the claims at the center of the excerpt amounted to “specific factual accusations of criminal misconduct” that were “categorically false.”
The letter, addressed to Richard A. Bernstein, vice president and deputy general counsel at Advance-Condé Nast, denies a series of allegations individually.
Kushner “was never a signatory to, never had access to, and never knew of any ‘Alpha’ account at First Abu Dhabi Bank,” the lawyers wrote. They also said he did not know of the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, that no “Beta” account was held for him at Israel’s central bank, and that he had no account in Cyprus.
“He never received, controlled, or directed money from any foreign government; never transferred funds to anyone from any such account; and never conditioned any action of the United States government on any benefit to himself,” the letter said.
The attorneys summarized Kushner’s denial in another passage: “There are no accounts and never were.”
The letter also challenged the evidence underlying the allegations, saying that despite repeated requests, Cole had “not provided a single bank statement, account document, or wire record substantiating his accusations.”
Kushner’s lawyers argued that the allegations were particularly implausible given the scrutiny he faced while serving in government, citing media investigations, congressional inquiries and a special counsel investigation.
The letter said Kushner provided more than 30 hours of testimony and filed financial disclosures during his government service, and asserted that none of those proceedings or filings revealed the alleged arrangements.
The attorneys also accused Vanity Fair of publishing the excerpt despite knowing that Kushner disputed the claims. According to the letter, Kushner’s counsel sent Cole and publisher Simon & Schuster letters dated July 30 and August 10 denying the allegations before Vanity Fair published the excerpt.
The October 23 letter demanded that Vanity Fair “immediately take down the excerpt” and preserve documents related to it, while warning that publication had exposed the outlet to what Kushner’s lawyers characterized as “serious legal risk.”
Attorney Chad Mizelle subsequently amplified the warning on X.
“We formally put Vanity Fair and Condé Nast on notice regarding the false and defamatory allegations published about our client, Jared Kushner,” Mizelle wrote in the post.
Mizelle said “serious questions” had been raised about the credibility of the reporting and reiterated the legal team’s objections to the allegations.
Kushner, 45, is a businessman and investor who served as a senior adviser to his father-in-law, Trump, during the president’s first term. Forbes says Kushner worked as CEO of his family’s real estate business, Kushner Companies, from 2008 to 2017 and founded the Miami-based private equity firm Affinity Partners in 2021.
Born January 10, 1981, in Livingston, New Jersey, Kushner is the eldest child of real estate developer Charles Kushner and Seryl Kushner, according to Encyclopaedia Britannica . The publication says he was raised in an Orthodox Jewish family, has three siblings and is the grandson of Holocaust survivors.
Kushner graduated from Harvard University in 2003 and earned a law degree and an MBA from New York University in 2007, according to Britannica . Forbes also lists a bachelor’s degree from Harvard and JD and MBA degrees from New York University among his credentials.
Forbes estimated Kushner’s real-time net worth at approximately $1 billion as of October 24, 2026, identifying real estate and private equity as the sources of his wealth.
Kushner married Ivanka Trump, Trump’s daughter, in 2009, according to Britannica . The couple have three children. Forbes likewise lists Kushner as married with three children.
Mizelle’s statement and the October 23 letter raise the prospect of litigation, but the reporting reviewed does not establish that a defamation lawsuit has been filed.
The letter demands that Vanity Fair remove the excerpt and preserve records related to its publication, potentially setting up a further legal dispute if the parties do not resolve their differences.
Meanwhile, Cole’s book was scheduled for release on October 27.

articles.title_orig: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
articles.title_zh: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
articles.content_orig:
The husband of a British woman who died rescuing their sons when they were swept away to sea in the Bahamas says she was a "hero... in life and in death".
Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been snorkelling with her family when the boys were swept away by a strong current, police said.
Although the children were rescued from the water off the island of Bimini on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.
Nathan Gregory said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable for our family".
"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post.
"I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together.
"My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."
Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".
In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".
He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."
In a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.
It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.
Mrs Gregory was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.
It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title_orig: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.title_zh: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
American households struggling with elevated living expenses and steep chocolate prices have driven a sluggish start to Halloween candy sales this year.
Figures from market research firm NielsenIQ reveal that candy purchases fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year.
An 11.7% drop in mid-September wiped out early-season sales gains recorded over the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said surging fuel costs have worsened concerns over affordability, curbing demand for treats.
As of Friday, the national average for regular gasoline stood at $4.29 a gallon, up nearly 40% from last year.
"I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food," Costagli said.
"Some of the decisions they're making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, 'I notice it's more expensive than last year,' it's, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I've paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’"
Costagli noted that small bags were the only package size seeing sales growth through mid-October, while large and extra-large sizes experienced the sharpest declines.
U.S. candy prices have outpaced general inflation for several years.
Government data shows candy and gum prices jumped 44% over a five-year period through September, while overall grocery costs rose 22.5% over the same timeframe.
Discount grocer Aldi advertised a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolates—including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers—for $19.87 this week.
That is nearly the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece pack five years ago.
High cocoa prices are the primary driver. Global cocoa costs hit a record $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 due to harsh weather in West Africa, which produces 70% of world supply, and speculative futures trading, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Although cocoa dropped to $3,241 per metric ton in March, prices rebounded in the spring after the Iran war disrupted fertilizer shipments to Africa.
The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to dampen output, bringing heat and dry conditions through February.
Costagli noted that demand remains weak even where prices have dropped. Non-chocolate treats like gummies and lollipops averaged $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, down roughly 3% from last year, without driving a surge in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser at Circana, said consumers are coping with high grocery bills by making smaller, more frequent shopping trips right before using items.
She questioned whether buyers are simply holding off until closer to Halloween.
"People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general," she said. "I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed."
The National Confectioners Association, representing producers such as Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic.
"We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong," the group said Friday in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
articles.title_zh: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
articles.content_orig:
JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.
You check your credit score, see nothing unusual and assume your identity is safe. But what if someone has already stolen your personal information and your credit report shows absolutely nothing? That's entirely possible.
Credit monitoring can help detect certain types of identity theft, particularly fraud involving new credit accounts. However, criminals can also target your existing bank accounts, retirement savings, government benefits and phone number without triggering a traditional credit alert. As a result, a clean credit report can give you a false sense of security. Here's what credit monitoring can catch, what it might miss and how to better protect yourself.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money
In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR
Reviewing financial statements regularly can help uncover suspicious activity that may never appear on your credit report. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Credit monitoring tracks changes to your credit file. Depending on the service, it can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit history.
These alerts can help you discover new account fraud before the damage grows. However, credit monitoring depends on information that lenders and other companies report to credit bureaus. Therefore, it cannot reliably detect identity theft that occurs entirely outside the credit reporting system.
Criminals have several ways to misuse your information, steal money or make you more vulnerable to fraud without triggering a traditional credit monitoring alert. Here are six situations worth watching for.
A criminal gains access to your existing checking account, savings account, retirement account or payment app. Because the account already exists, the takeover may never appear on your credit report. Instead, you might first discover the theft through an unfamiliar transaction or a notification from your financial institution.
Someone uses your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return or claim government benefits. You may receive an IRS notice about a tax return you never filed. Alternatively, you could discover unemployment benefits claimed in your name. Neither situation necessarily changes your credit score.
A thief uses your health insurance information to receive medical care, prescriptions or equipment. You might then receive bills for services you never used. Even worse, someone else's medical information could end up in your records. Traditional credit monitoring generally will not detect the misuse itself, although unpaid debts could eventually create other financial complications.
Criminals may convince your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card or device they control. Once they have your number, they may intercept certain verification codes and attempt to access your accounts. A sudden loss of cellular service could be an early warning sign, especially if you did not request a change.
A scammer tricks you into authorizing a wire transfer, sending money through a payment app or purchasing gift cards. Because you initiated the payment, even under false pretenses, traditional credit monitoring may have no indication that anything happened. Your financial institution might have separate fraud detection systems, but those protections vary.
Your name, phone number, address and other personal details may appear on people-search websites or data broker databases. Criminals can use that information to create convincing phishing messages or impersonation scams. Although the exposure itself does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity, it can make you a more attractive target. The Federal Trade Commission identifies unauthorized bank withdrawals, unfamiliar medical bills and fraudulent tax filings among the warning signs of identity theft.
SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW
Criminals can access existing financial accounts or misuse payment information without triggering traditional credit monitoring alerts. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A credit score provides a snapshot of your creditworthiness based on information in your credit file. It does not show every account you own, or every place someone might use your personal information. For example, someone could access your retirement account while your credit score remains unchanged.
Similarly, criminals might use your phone number to get into an existing account without ever applying for credit. That's why it's important to review your actual credit reports rather than relying on your score alone. Even then, you'll need to check your other accounts separately.
Fortunately, you can look for suspicious activity without paying for an expensive monitoring service. Start with these six habits.
Check your bank statements, investment accounts, retirement accounts and payment apps for unfamiliar transactions. Also, enable transaction and security alerts whenever your financial institutions offer them.
Pay attention to IRS notices about returns you did not file or income from employers you don't recognize. You can also review your federal tax account through the official IRS website at irs.gov/ . You can also request a free six-digit Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. This helps prevent someone else from filing a fraudulent federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each year.
Review your earnings history periodically to see whether it matches your actual employment. You can access your information through your my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Unexpected earnings may require further investigation.
Look for unfamiliar medical appointments, prescriptions, procedures or insurance claims. If something looks suspicious, contact your health insurance company or medical provider directly.
Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM swap safeguards. Additionally, consider using an authenticator app or security key instead of text-message verification when available.
Search for your name, phone number and address to identify information exposed through people-search websites. You can request removal from individual sites or consider a reputable data removal service.
Pro tip: Choose one day each month to review your accounts and important records. You can combine it with a bill-payment routine to make the habit easier to maintain.
Monitoring your online accounts and enabling security alerts can help you spot potential identity theft before the damage grows. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Credit monitoring remains useful, but it cannot catch every type of identity theft. Some identity theft protection services offer broader monitoring that can help identify suspicious activity involving financial accounts, personal information and online accounts. However, the features and level of protection depend on the provider and plan you choose.
Before signing up, compare the features, coverage limits and costs. Pay attention to which financial accounts qualify for monitoring and whether the service offers restoration assistance if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border on Oct. 24, monitoring channels reported.
A fire first broke out at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
The facility is one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, and the company behind Omsky Kauchuk says the site is a leading producer of synthetic rubber, organic synthesis products, and methyl tert-butyl ether, an additive used to refine gasoline.
The plant is part of Russia's supply chain for rocket fuel, including for the Iskander ballistic missile used in fatal attacks against Ukraine, Exilenova Plus said.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25. At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22.
Later, a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Ozon was also hit in the Ukrainian drone attack, Exilenova Plus reported .
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaliy Khotsenko confirmed that the region was targeted by Ukrainian drones, saying that a logistics hub in the city of Omsk was hit.

articles.title_orig: Three days before election, Netanyahu warns Iran is preparing to destroy Israel
articles.title_zh: Three days before election, Netanyahu warns Iran is preparing to destroy Israel
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
An Israeli special operations veteran urged the United States and Israel on Friday to focus future military strikes on preventing Iran from rebuilding its nuclear and missile capabilities.
Aaron Cohen, founder of Gideon, told FOX Business' "Kudlow" that previous U.S. and Israeli operations had significantly weakened Iran's military infrastructure, but warned that Tehran could restore its capabilities without continued pressure.
Cohen pointed to reported activity at Iran's underground Eagle 44 military base and changes in the country's defense leadership as possible signs of rebuilding efforts. He argued that future operations should prioritize disrupting Iran's ability to replenish military equipment and infrastructure.
His comments come as President Donald Trump has raised the possibility of additional strikes against Iran following the November midterm elections, although no new military operation has been announced.
Brent crude briefly topped $117 a barrel Friday as uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict continued to weigh on global energy markets.
The international oil benchmark settled at $116.72 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, closed at $103.27 after climbing above $103 during the trading session.
The latest price movements come as commercial vessels continue to face security threats in the Strait of Hormuz, a major shipping corridor for global oil supplies.
President Donald Trump's administration has maintained a naval blockade targeting Iranian oil exports, while the president has left open the possibility of additional military strikes against Tehran.
International nuclear inspectors could play a central role in a future agreement between the United States and Iran, with the United Nations ' nuclear watchdog signaling Friday that it has completed much of the preparation needed to verify Tehran's nuclear activities.
Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told the U.N. General Assembly in New York that the agency is prepared to carry out independent monitoring if Washington and Tehran reach a diplomatic agreement.
Grossi emphasized that a lasting resolution to the dispute over Iran's nuclear program would require international oversight, making verification a key component of any potential deal.
The IAEA chief also expressed optimism about diplomatic efforts involving Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Egypt, which have supported negotiations between the United States and Iran.
His remarks come as President Donald Trump has raised the possibility of additional military strikes against Iran if Tehran does not reach an agreement with Washington.
While the IAEA says its technical preparations are largely complete, no new agreement authorizing inspections has been announced.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is preparing to host Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow next week, adding another round of high-level diplomacy between the two countries as Tehran faces continued U.S. military and economic pressure.
The upcoming visit was confirmed by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Reuters reported. It comes just days after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov traveled to Tehran for discussions with Iranian officials.
The diplomatic activity highlights the close relationship between Moscow and Tehran, even as President Donald Trump has questioned how much assistance Russia is providing Iran during the conflict.
Araghchi has maintained that relations between the two countries are stronger than ever, according to Reuters.
The meeting would mark Pezeshkian's first visit with Putin in Russia since the conflict began, although the two leaders have held talks elsewhere in recent months, including in Turkmenistan earlier in October and Kyrgyzstan in September.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have rebounded above pre-conflict levels despite Iran's efforts to disrupt energy shipments through the region.
In a post on X, Bessent shared a Treasury Department chart showing crude oil and condensate exports through the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea recovering to approximately 17 million to 18 million barrels per day.
The chart shows shipments plunged earlier this year before gradually recovering, with the latest figures exceeding the January-February 2026 average.
Bessent credited the rebound as evidence that Iran has failed to halt energy shipments to international markets despite attacks on commercial vessels and continued tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
The development comes as the Trump administration maintains economic pressure on Tehran through a U.S. naval blockade aimed at restricting Iranian oil exports while allowing other energy shipments to continue.
A 2014 conference in Tehran attended by Code Pink co-founder Medea Benjamin was later sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department over allegations that it helped Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) recruit foreign intelligence assets, according to a report by The Telegraph.
The Treasury Department sanctioned the New Horizon organization in 2019, accusing it of facilitating intelligence gathering and recruitment on behalf of the IRGC's Quds Force.
Benjamin was photographed at the conference with Nader Talebzadeh and Hamed Ghashghavi, two men whom U.S. authorities later identified as intermediaries involved in identifying potential foreign recruits, The Telegraph reported.
The report also cited an intelligence source who alleged that Iran considered Benjamin an asset because of her public advocacy. The characterization does not, by itself, establish that Benjamin knowingly cooperated with Iranian intelligence.
Benjamin returned to Iran in 2019 as part of a 28-member Code Pink delegation that met with then-Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif.
Internet connectivity across the Persian Gulf could face disruptions if fighting between Iran and the United States resumes, with Iranian security officials reportedly considering attacks on underwater communications cables.
The potential consequences could be concentrated in the region rather than felt worldwide. Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography, told Reuters that less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The assessment comes as two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters that Tehran has prepared plans to damage undersea communications infrastructure in response to renewed U.S. and Israeli military strikes.
One official also described plans to interfere with repairs, potentially extending service disruptions. Neither official identified specific cables or explained how Iran would carry out the attacks.
The reported threat comes as President Donald Trump has suggested the U.S. could launch additional military operations against Iran if Tehran does not reach an agreement with Washington.
Internet and telecommunications networks in the Persian Gulf could become targets of Iranian retaliation if President Donald Trump orders additional military strikes against Tehran, according to a Reuters report Friday.
Two senior Iranian security officials told the news agency that Tehran has prepared contingency plans involving underwater communications cables, potentially threatening connectivity across the region.
The reported plans also include obstructing repairs to damaged infrastructure, which could extend disruptions to internet and other communications services.
The warning comes as Trump has raised the possibility of another round of Operation Epic Fury strikes against Iran , suggesting Friday that additional military action remains an option if Tehran does not reach an agreement with Washington.
Reuters reported that the Iranian officials did not identify specific cables or provide details about how the attacks would be carried out.

articles.title_orig: Six Flags adding seat belts to Goliath rollercoaster following death
articles.title_zh: Six Flags adding seat belts to Goliath rollercoaster following death
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags has announced it will be adding seat belts to some of its rollercoasters after a man fell to his death on the Goliath ride in the US state of Georgia earlier this month.
The company's CEO John Reilly said in a letter to customers late on Friday that the company is reinforcing safety measure across its parks, including adding seat belts to Goliath and similar rides, which already feature lap bar restraints.
The chain of amusement parks has 34 locations across North America, with over 220 rollercoasters in total.
Georgia's Goliath ride will remain closed pending safety reviews and out of an abundance of caution, so will eight other rides at five other parks, Reilly added.
The CEO also said the company has hired independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across all its amusement parks. The company is committed to taking action based on the experts' findings and will share progress updates, he said.
On 12 October, a 42-year-old man named Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed at Six Flags Over Georgia after being ejected from the Goliath, police have said. Four other passengers were injured as he fell.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"Our hearts remain with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, those injured, and everyone impacted by the tragic incident," Reilly said in his letter.
"What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags," he added.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five
Over 28 million guests visit Six Flags locations every year, according to the company's website.
October's fatal incident was not the first time a passenger has been hurt at one of the parks.
An Iraq War veteran died in 2011 after being ejected from a ride in New York. In 2013, a woman died after slipping from her restraints and falling 75 feet from a coaster in Texas.
In 2022, a 22-year-old man died from a brain injury after riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California. His family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.

articles.title_orig: The Rare-Earth Vultures Harvesting Metals From America’s Old Wind Turbines
articles.title_zh: The Rare-Earth Vultures Harvesting Metals From America’s Old Wind Turbines
articles.content_orig:
The technologies transforming modern industry depend on materials that rarely receive the same attention as the innovations they make possible. Artificial intelligence, robotics, electric vehicles, advanced aerospace systems, and high-performance electronics all rely on sophisticated components whose production requires access to specialized minerals.
Perhaps the most strategically important are rare earth elements, particularly those used in high-performance permanent magnets. And while the technology industry continues pushing the boundaries of what machines can accomplish, another challenge is gaining urgency: finding dependable new sources of the materials needed to manufacture them.
China dominates much of the world’s rare earth processing and magnet production, creating a concentrated supply chain that governments and manufacturers are increasingly determined to diversify.
That effort is directing attention toward resource-rich countries such as Brazil. But discovering new mineral deposits is only part of the solution.
The next important technological advances may come from finding better ways to recover the minerals already being discovered.
Why Rare Earth Recovery Technology Matters
Rare earth elements aren’t necessarily rare in Earth’s crust. The difficulty often lies in identifying deposits with useful concentrations of valuable elements and developing efficient methods to separate and recover them.
Terbium and dysprosium illustrate the challenge. These heavy rare earth elements help certain permanent magnets retain their strength at elevated temperatures, making them valuable in electric vehicle motors, industrial robotics, wind turbines, and aerospace equipment.
For manufacturers, access to these materials is closely connected to product performance and supply reliability. For companies developing new mineral resources, the question becomes how to extract them in ways that are technically practical, environmentally manageable, and potentially commercially viable.
One area attracting attention is ionic adsorption clay, a type of rare earth-bearing deposit in which certain elements can be recovered through chemical leaching.
Unlike conventional hard-rock mining, some ionic clay deposits may offer opportunities to investigate alternative extraction approaches, potentially reducing the amount of material that must be excavated and processed.
And in Brazil, researchers are exploring what those possibilities could mean for future rare earth supplies.
A Brazilian Project Combining Scale With Technical Progress
Among the companies investigating these opportunities is IMC Rare Earths Ltd. (NYSE American: IMC), which is advancing its Itarantim rare earth project across portions of Bahia and Minas Gerais.
Itarantim hosts a reported 1.1-billion-tonne inferred mineral resource containing the four principal magnet rare earth elements: neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
That geological scale provides a strong foundation for exploration, but it’s the company’s recent metallurgical testing that adds another dimension to the project.
In September, laboratory work conducted with Brazil’s IFRN and CT Mineral reported terbium recovery reaching 95.2% in the best-performing test , with an average recovery of 81.1% in the reported composite. The company also produced a mixed rare earth carbonate, an intermediate material that can be further processed into separated rare earth products.
Separate research at the University of Brighton in the United Kingdom recovered 73% of the total rare earth elements tested, excluding cerium, using an acidified magnesium sulfate solution. The same testing recovered 71.4% of terbium and 70.5% of dysprosium.
These results were obtained under different laboratory conditions and should not be treated as interchangeable recovery rates. Nevertheless, they show how Itarantim’s mineralization responds to potential extraction methods.
And that information is central to evaluating what comes next.
Could Rare Earths Be Recovered Through Wells?
One of the more intriguing possibilities emerging from testing is in-situ recovery .
Rather than excavating large volumes of rare earth-bearing clay, the proposed method involves injecting a suitable solution through injection wells, letting it interact with the mineralized material, and recovering the resulting rare earth-bearing liquid through extraction wells.
The minerals would then undergo further processing to produce intermediate materials suitable for eventual refining.
If successfully demonstrated under field conditions, this approach could potentially reduce excavation, material transportation, and the need for extensive tailings storage. It might also offer advantages in surface disturbance and infrastructure requirements compared with certain conventional mining methods.
The technology is not yet commercially validated at Itarantim. Field testing must establish whether fluids can move effectively through the deposit, remain controlled, and be recovered reliably.
But the laboratory findings provide a reason to investigate those possibilities further.
Another encouraging observation concerns the composition of the recovered solutions. In the University of Brighton tests, uranium and thorium remained below detection limits in the leachate. IMC has also reported negligible deleterious elements in certain tested solutions.
These results do not establish that the entire deposit is free of radioactivity. They do, however, provide potentially useful information for researchers, regulators, and development partners assessing processing requirements, environmental considerations, and future waste management.
As the technology becomes increasingly focused on efficiency and resource management, those characteristics could become important as testing advances.
New Discoveries Expand the Scientific Questions
While the metallurgical work continues, IMC is also investigating mineralization beyond its existing resource boundaries.
On October 8, the company announced a new high-grade, terbium-rich zone at Block H, where drilling identified seven meters of mineralization beginning just two meters below the surface, including a higher-grade three-meter section.
Preliminary testing recovered 64% to 83% of terbium from samples taken from the upper portion of the enriched zone.
The discovery lies outside Itarantim’s currently defined resource, creating another area for exploration. At Block D, drilling has also identified 20 meters of continuous mineralization, with additional work planned to investigate its extent.
Together, these findings are helping researchers examine both the deposit’s geological characteristics and recovery methods suitable for different mineralized areas.
IMC has engaged ANSTO Minerals in Australia for further metallurgical studies and is evaluating potential processing approaches, including in-situ, vat, and heap leaching.
Next stages will include additional resource definition, engineering evaluation, field testing, and potential partnerships with industrial and government organizations that can support future development.
The Technology Behind a More Diversified Supply Chain
The global effort to diversify rare earth supplies is often discussed in terms of geopolitics and mineral discoveries. Yet processing technology may prove equally important.
A large mineral resource cannot contribute to manufacturing supply chains unless its valuable elements can be recovered, refined, and delivered in forms that industry can use.
That makes the work taking place at projects such as Itarantim relevant beyond the mining sector. Laboratory research, chemical processing, geological modeling, and engineering innovation all support efforts to establish new sources of materials essential to advanced technology.
Brazil’s substantial rare earth potential offers opportunities to continue that work, while international cooperation could connect emerging mineral projects with the processing

articles.title_orig: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA: "Now is the time"
articles.title_zh: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA: "Now is the time"
articles.content_orig:
FORT MYERS, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Friday used a campaign ​rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled.
In a 90-minute speech in Fort Myers, Trump repeated ‌more military action against Iran may lie ahead as he tries to address the causes of a spike in oil prices that has put ⁠Republicans on the defensive ahead of the Nov. 3 ​midterm elections.
With an eye toward the senior Americans ⁠who live in Florida, Trump said he planned to spend $250 million to hire at least 5,000 new nurses in ‌elder care facilities all across ‌America.
While the Iran war has no end in sight, Trump talked tough about Cuba, part ⁠of a pattern of putting pressure on the communist government there ⁠after ousting the leader of Venezuela early this year .
Trump, who won 68% of the Cuban American vote in Florida in the 2024 election, said American naval forces from Iran will stop at Cuba on the way home.
"We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," he said.
Secretary ‌of State Marco Rubio, a former senator from Florida, has been handling ​much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump.
"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time," Rubio said on X on Friday, urging those disappointed by Cuba's government "to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA." His post did not elaborate.
Trump's rally was intended to boost the electoral prospects of Florida Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running for governor against Democrat David Jolly.
His speech, the latest in a near-daily blitz of campaign rallies in largely friendly areas, rambled from ​topic to topic such as the size of his crowds and his White House renovations.
Trump has increased pressure on Cuba in ‌his second term. In ‌September, he labeled ⁠Cuba a "failed state" at the United Nations General Assembly and said, "Freedom will be coming to Cuba," prompting a walkout by the Cuban delegation.
Trump has openly stated that his goal is to fundamentally change Cuba's government. A U.S.-imposed oil blockade has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
U.N. ‌human rights experts have condemned the ​oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights ‌advocates say the Trump administration's threats ⁠have echoed an imperialist ​approach.
Contributing: Kanishka Singh

articles.title_orig: ‘Total Meltdown’ in Riskiest Debt Unnerves Market: Credit Weekly
articles.title_zh: ‘Total Meltdown’ in Riskiest Debt Unnerves Market: Credit Weekly
articles.content_orig:
Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.
Hesitancy to issue some securitizations in a tougher market is intensifying the need for nonbank mortgage lenders to find ways to cope with shifting investor demand.
Figure recently backed off on issuing a private-label securitization, Freddie Mac reportedly paused a multifamily mortgage transaction and at least one two commercial real estate deals stalled due to investor interest in being paid to take on mortgage risk in a bond market where Treasury yields have been volatile, according to Bloomberg reports.
The circumstances demonstrate why lenders increasingly benefit by having multiple markets and investors ready to potentially buy their loans.
"Don't have just one outlet for the product. Make sure you have at least two or three, so that if something does go bad with the one investor's demand, you have others," Nathan Regehr, principal at Regehr Capital Markets Advisory, said in an interview.
Figure's decision to back off a securitization, which it confirmed occurred because it got a better price in the whole loan market, supports that point.
The fintech company also noted that it operates a private credit market aimed at giving other lenders multiple loan outlets and recently has split its activity between whole loan and securitized markets.
"Since the start of September, we've completed more than $1 billion across three securitizations and another $1 billion across 24 whole-loan sales," Figure said in an emailed statement.
Figure also noted recently in an X post that it recently found "institutional whole-loan bids are offering better pricing than securitization markets."
However, other experts said the whole loan bid's relative attractiveness to securitizations varies depending on the product and situation. Also, whole loan bidders aren't necessarily offering a premium in all circumstances.
"The largest buyers of, for example, non-QM, are insurance companies, all of whom know the structured market very well," David Akre, principal, Whole Loan Capital, said in an email, adding that this means "the odds of getting a better execution in whole loans are slim."
Why some deals are stalling, other private mortgage-related securitizations are still coming to market, so lenders should compare what's offered in that market to whole loan executions for themselves.
"I hear those same anecdotes of some non-agency securitizations being delayed, but I think you're continuing to see a fairly significant volume being done," said Eric Hagen, managing director at BTIG, in an interview.
Specified pools are another area where there have been reports of deals being disrupted or priced lower as the Fed has hiked rates but some investor interest persists.
"In every market, some spec pools are going to do well," Regehr said. "New York loans are performing better and they have larger loan amounts and lower risk, so those still might get pay-ups."
However, some spec pools are in a situation where the investor may not really want the product anymore.
"In this kind of market, you either have to accept the price or maybe say no and come back later if you can hold on to those pools for a little bit on your warehouse line," Regehr said. "If your borrowing cost is significantly lower than the interest rates on the loan, you might as well keep the loan there."
While waiting to sell or securitize until the market improves can have some benefits, it also may have some downsides.
The cost to warehouse the loan is one to consider. The other is how a delay affects counterparties and whether or not there are negative impacts that affect the business relationship in the future.
"It might affect them going forward," Walt Schmidt, senior vice president, mortgage strategies, at FHN Financial said in an interview.
More than half of potential buyers expect mortgage rates to be higher within the next year, up 12 percentage points from a year ago, an industry survey found.
Economic factors may limit growth in renovation spending, but the need for improvements to existing housing should spur demand, an industry leader says.
The company expects to report net income between $205 million and $220 million, with positive servicing results offset by an originations miss, analysts said.
The lender reported a significant upturn in profits during the third quarter, as rising servicing income offset a pullback in new originations.
A judge ordered Equity Prime Mortgage to pay over $1.3 million in a case that scrutinized its contracts, and subservicing relationship, with counterparties.
Affiliating with a professional sports team or arena can put your company name in front of consumers in ways that can outlast interest rate shifts.

articles.title_orig: AI tool REA cracks paid software: Is the software industry's business model coming to an end?
articles.title_zh: AI tool REA cracks paid software: Is the software industry's business model coming to an end?
articles.content_orig:
It was predicted, just in a slightly different way: rather than having to buy software in the long run, you'd simply have your AI agents program the features you need. Now there's another development: take an expensive paid app on your PC, run REA on it, and your AI can learn the professional tool's entire codebase and functionality before rebuilding it as open-source software.
A few days ago, we reported on programmer and entrepreneur Brandon Thomas, who, frustrated with Adobe, decided to recreate almost the entire Adobe suite as open-source software under the project name ArtCraft, making it freely available to everyone. This includes Premiere, After Effects, and more. Thomas has years of programming experience, but what if anyone could do this soon?
That's where the new open-source tool REA comes in. The acronym stands for Reverse Engineer Anything. REA connects AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
REA analyzes software based on instructions given in natural language to understand how it works, even when the original source code isn't available. While REA can't always recover the original source code exactly, it can reconstruct readable code based on the software's functionality. This reconstruction gives an AI agent enough information to replicate parts of the software, ideally achieving comparable results with newly written code. The result is a custom implementation that delivers the same functionality.
Using a new codebase for the implementation could also make copyright enforcement more difficult in practice, since the original source code hasn't actually been stolen. And that's precisely where the potential for market disruption lies. Functionally recreating software is legally different from copying its protected source code.
REA significantly lowers the barrier to entry, and this app is almost certainly just the beginning. Instead of having to understand everything yourself, you can ask the AI questions and give it tasks in natural language. However, a fair amount of technical knowledge is still required for now, including installation, working with the tools, and verifying the results. That said, YouTube and other platforms promise easy-to-follow tutorials that can help users get around some of these hurdles.
More accessible reverse engineering could mark a major technological leap. Recreating software is becoming cheaper. But that doesn't automatically mean smaller players will necessarily benefit. At the same time, competition could intensify, shifting the focus away from features and exclusive code toward usability, reliability, data, ecosystems, customer support, trust, and ongoing development. This is where large corporations have an advantage, potentially putting even more pressure on smaller developers.
I didn't try REA with the powerful Claude Code because it's too expensive for me. Instead, I'm using the ad-supported, free app Freebuff (don't provide sensible data!).
I instructed the AI to install REA and all its dependencies, along with MCP and Ghidra. From there, the entire process ran automatically, and I didn't have to do anything else.
Next, I wanted to recreate an app. It shouldn't be as complicated as a game, but not as simple as a calculator either. The VLC Media Player came to mind, so I entered the following prompt:
The agent got to work, asked me three more questions, and finished after about 10 to 15 minutes. I had my own VLC clone. I was also informed that it used Chromium rather than libVLC as its engine, meaning some video formats wouldn't work. That could be changed, though.
The “Own Player” worked right from the start. I simply dragged an MP3 file into the window, and playback began immediately. I could also open folders, although subfolders weren't included. Keyboard shortcuts for seeking, muting, and other functions worked perfectly. The only issue was that fullscreen mode displayed a black screen.
Overall, though, the result was impressive for just a few minutes of work. Once everything was installed, virtually all it took to create an app was a single prompt and answers to three multiple-choice questions.
Reverse engineering is nothing new. But AI is lowering the barriers to entry and making the process increasingly straightforward, even for non-coders. And that's precisely what could put software copyright law to the test: if anyone can easily recreate their own apps from paid software, this could threaten software vendors' business models.
Not every copy is legal, of course, but under certain conditions, functionality can be recreated without using the original code. As a result, the code that software vendors spent so much money developing could lose some of its value as a competitive advantage, even if their copyrights remain untouched. This could reshape the software market in the long term, potentially in disruptive ways.
In the past, you bought software and owned a copy. Then came the subscription era, when software was licensed for use rather than sold outright. If everyone can build their own apps—or recreate existing ones—the software licensing model will likely be affected as well.

articles.title_orig: New ‘Mass Effect 5’ Details Emerge After Cancellation, And It Sounds Great
articles.title_zh: New ‘Mass Effect 5’ Details Emerge After Cancellation, And It Sounds Great
articles.content_orig:
Those mourning yesterday’s shuttering of highly praised and influential developer BioWare also had to deal with the cancellation of the next Mass Effect game, which was first teased back in 2020 . Today, we got our best look at what that game could have been with a short, leaked trailer for Mass Effect: Universe .
In the roughly two-minute montage—which describes itself as “in-engine footage from our small team” that “uses our pre-production assets”—an ex-military officer wearing an N7 trenchcoat (similar to the one seen in that 2020 teaser) encounters an Asari at a bar. He talks of his frustration with military life—“by the time you put out one fire, another had already started”—before discussing his new line of work “stopping [the fires] before they start” and “making the choices no one else is willing to make. Going where others are afraid to go.”
Mass Effect: Universe Trailer by u/Random_Hyabusa_Ninja in masseffect
As the intriguing Asari at the bar reveals herself to be the one who metaphorically “start[s] the fires,” N7 allies reveal themselves as backup. The cutscene transitions seamlessly into an all-out group gunfight in the bar, complete with hostiles being stuck in place inside mass effect fields and others being crushed by furniture brought down on top of them.
The action-packed bar scene is interspersed with short vignettes from around the game’s universe, including a hovercraft speeding over an icy planet, an examination of a truly gigantic alien suspended in a glass cylinder, and a team looking at a holographic map dotted with dozens of points of interest.
The existence of the internal Mass Effect: Universe trailer was first revealed by an anonymous Reddit poster yesterday and then confirmed by IGN early Thursday morning. The trailer video appeared on Reddit slightly before noon Eastern time, with mods there saying they couldn’t “independently verify the authenticity” but that it “seems legitimate.” Within hours, both IGN and Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier had confirmed that the trailer was authentic and came from someone inside EA.
Following yesterday’s BioWare closure announcement, sci-fi authors Catherynne M. Valente and Derek Kunsken both revealed they had been working on the game for years. “It was one of the greatest privileges & GLORIOUS challenges of my life. I smiled every day. I worked HARD for the fans, every day,” Valente wrote. “What we were cooking was really cool,” Kunsken added.
Despite the existence of a 6-year-old teaser for the game, EA executives Cam Weber and David Tinson said in a memo to staff yesterday that there was only “a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect .” The decision “not to move forward with this development” led to BioWare’s closure, which the note calls “a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly.”
In an N7 Day blog post last year , Executive Producer Mike Gamble said, “The team is heads-down and focused exclusively on Mass Effect . We have a lot of universe to cover, lots of features to build, and lots of romances to figure out. We’re excited by what we’re building, and we promise you: when we’re ready, it’ll be a lot of fun to show.”
“Your support has meant everything to me over the past 17 years at BioWare,” Gamble wrote yesterday on social media .
Despite the game’s cancellation, the Mass Effect universe will still be represented on streaming TV screens. IGN cites “sources inside Prime Video” in reporting that the streaming series first announced in 2024 is still in active development.
As for the series’s future in gaming, an Internet petition has predictably popped up urging EA to continue funding development of the series or license the IP to an outside studio. The petition has nearly 17,500 signatories as of this writing, though those petitioners face an uphill battle convincing EA’s new private ownership to focus on a massive narrative action RPG and not more profitable franchises like Battlefield , The Sims , and annual sports releases.

A Texas woman who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 now says through tears that she will ânever vote for that man again.â
In an emotional interview, Jessica Vuittonet, a Hispanic coffee shop owner in San Benito, ten miles north of the southern border, tells CBS News she did not believe Trumpâs sweeping migrant crackdown would impact her own family and other innocent immigrants.
âI know he was going to start deporting people,â she said. âBut not innocent peopleânot hardworking people.â
Jessica Vuittonet says her brother, who does not have a criminal record, has been detained by ICE.
Vuittonet says her brother is among those arrested by Trumpâs immigration goons. She says she voted for Trump for religious reasons, but now realizes Trumpâs policies are âheartbreaking.â
âItâs hardworking men that are being detained by ICE, not criminals,â she said. âThat are up in the roofs, that are doing somebodyâs driveway, that are cutting somebodyâs grass, that are literally having a work truck to go work. Where are the criminals you said you were going to arrest? Yes, thereâs a few that youâve done, but the majority have been hardworking people.â
She continued, âHardworking women. I just want to tear upâwomen that Iâve seen with their children, walking every day to school. Whereâs your mom? Kids staying behindâbroken families, it is just heartbreaking.â
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Trumpâs violent crackdown, which has reportedly led to around 980,000 people being deported , most of whom have no criminal record, has sparked regret among many Trump voters who wanted to see criminals removed from the countryânot innocent families violently split apart.
Benny Melendez, who has installed fences on construction sites he manages to protect his workers from ICE, says he also regrets voting for Trumpâjust as he regretted voting for Biden in 2020.
Melendez tells CBS News that so many arrests in his Texas community have made it hard to find workers, and building a house can take twice as long because of a lack of manpower. According to TRAC , Texas, a state that has voted for Trump in all three of his presidential elections, has more immigration detentions than any other state.
Trumpâs approval rating has fallen to a record low of 32 percent, according to CNN , just weeks ahead of the midterms that are expected to be a bloodbath for Republicans, who are at serious risk of losing their majorities in both the House and Senate.
The economy has proven to be the most stubborn issue for most Americans, with two-thirds of voters, and one-third of Republicans , saying the president has made economic conditions worse.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stands with White House Border Czar Tom Homan, and Attorney General Pam Bondi before former U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin is sworn in as the next secretary of the Department of Homeland Security in the Oval Office at the White House on March 24, 2026.
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
While polling has suggested that immigration is unlikely to be a definitional issue ahead of Novemberâs elections, Michigan State University political scientist Matthew Grossman told The Guardian that Trumpâs deportation policies were part of a general feeling of the president having â gone too far ,â a sentiment also seen in terms of the Iran war and tariffs .
However, the issue hasnât fazed White House border czar Tom Homan: âMy job as a border czar is to keep that border secure and enforce immigration law,â he told CBS News earlier this month. âI particularly donât care about midterms.â

articles.title_orig: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
articles.title_zh: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
articles.content_orig:
A drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca , a study found.
Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.
The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.
That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed.
"I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.
The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility."
The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.
Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.
Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.
He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years.
Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.
Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone.
Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.
Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it.
Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer.
Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.
The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches.
Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own.
She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread.
In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since.
"I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

articles.title_orig: 'The transit world is where innovation goes to die' — The U.S. lags far behind on using driverless trains, but new projects could open the floodgates
articles.title_zh: 'The transit world is where innovation goes to die' — The U.S. lags far behind on using driverless trains, but new projects could open the floodgates
articles.content_orig:
Even as automated vehicles such as robotaxis grow more prevalent in the U.S., almost every mass transit system still requires a driver or operator on board. Two major cities are seeking to change that.
Officials in Washington, D.C., recently advanced a plan that could let computers fully control one of its subways, and Los Angeles is seeking to build a new, completely automated line. Honolulu already has one.
The Washington and LA projects, which would take years to implement and still face financial and technical hurdles, come amid an already fierce debate over the safety risks and benefits of automated trains and whether the substantial upfront expense is worth the long-term savings in labor costs.
Supporters call the push long overdue, pointing out that American cities lag far behind numerous places across the world that run unattended subways, metros or buses, including several cities in Europe and Asia, as well as major systems in Canada, Australia, South America and the Middle East.
“It should be much harder to automate something that’s on-road, that has all of these various obstacles coming at it, compared to a fixed-rail system,” said Baruch Feigenbaum, senior managing director of transportation policy at the Reason Foundation, a libertarian think tank that has advocated for transit automation. “I don’t know a nice way to say this, but basically the transit world is where innovation goes to die.”
Only in recent years have on-road vehicles from such companies as Waymo, Tesla and Zoox taken the automation lead in the U.S. ahead of transit systems using a track. In fact, although operators have always been part of the Metro subway system in Washington, D.C., trains ran with some automated features when it opened 50 years ago. After a 2009 fatal crash, those were turned off, then restored over the past two years.
Now, officials in the nation’s capital have renewed their push for automation on Metro’s Red Line. And an environmental review is underway in Los Angeles for an automated track for a new underground line of its heavy-rail system that would cut through the rough terrain of the Santa Monica Mountains.
Honolulu is already running an elevated driverless line — the most expansive automated transit system in the U.S. It’ll stretch 19 miles when completed, surpassing the elevated driverless trains Detroit and Miami opened as pilot projects in the 1980s, a monorail connecting hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and smaller systems that carry passengers between airport terminals.
An automated monorail that once ran in Memphis, Tennessee, closed down years ago. And the driverless Jacksonville Skyway will indefinitely halt operations soon due to budget cuts, despite initial plans for an even larger automated system.
After nine people were killed and many others injured in the 2009 train collision near the Fort Totten station on the D.C. Red Line, the National Transportation Safety Board blamed the crash on a maintenance problem in the automated signaling system that separates trains from one another.
Randy Clarke, CEO of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority , pointed out in an interview with The Associated Press that the issue in Fort Totten had nothing to do with the cruise control-like system that was restored on the Red Line in 2024 and the other Metro lines last year. Still, he acknowledged that for many years the crash “paralyzed” Metro’s plans for further automation.
“That was a big failure, there’s no question. We do not do anything like that now,” said Clarke, who called the current system “highly regulated, highly documented, very proficient.”
Trains could conceivably run without a human worker inside the cab as early as 2033 under the nearly $1 billion plan Metro’s Board of Directors backed in April to upgrade the Red Line with safety features including protective barriers that prevent passengers from getting onto the tracks.
Clarke said that even if workers aren’t needed to physically run the trains, they will be needed to maintain the tracks and respond to emergencies.
Unions have been critics of automation. John Samuelsen, a former worker in the New York subway system who now serves as international president of the Transport Workers Union, said unions have fought off automation efforts in New York and elsewhere, calling them “a catastrophe waiting to happen.”
“Passengers will be left dealing with a self-evacuation, which is a disaster in a system which runs on a third rail,” Samuelsen said.
To alleviate massive traffic bottlenecks for commuters, Honolulu opened its Skyline automated light metro transit system three years ago and expanded it last year.
Vance Tsuda, the system’s project director, said there hasn’t been a single crash or injury associated with automation. Even hybrid systems are less safe than a completely automated one, he said, arguing that a human is far more likely to overlook something like an open door and prematurely clear a train for departure.
“If you have somebody making that decision, they could make a wrong decision,” Tsuda said.
But David King, an associate professor of urban planning at Arizona State University who has researched automated transportation, said the success rate has to remain perfect to keep the public trust. That’s why the Fort Totten crash and others involving automation put the technology so far behind, he said.
“We allow a certain amount of failure with private industry that we don’t tolerate when the state does it,” said King, citing the several rockets blown up by Elon Musk’s SpaceX — a record he argues would cripple NASA’s budget if it happened in the public sector.
Perhaps the most ambitious transit automation effort being pursued in the U.S. is the subway line Los Angeles officials voted to recommend beneath the Santa Monica Mountains. The area is one of the most notorious traffic headaches in the country, with the mountains dividing the bustling Westside employment hub from the San Fernando Valley.
There’s already a subway system under the same mountain range near Hollywood, but that one has a driver onboard. The new proposal, which is undergoing an environmental review, would use shorter, more frequent trains, said Cecily Way, who oversees planning for the Sepulveda Project for LA Metro.
Like the project in Washington, the new line in Los Angeles would feature station doors to protect passengers on the platform from oncoming trains.
Feigenbaum with the Reason Foundation said that automation of a major transit line such as in Los Angeles or Washington could open the floodgates for other cities to follow.
“It sends a signal that this is technologically doable and this is something that maybe other systems are going to want to strive for,” he said.
