articles.title_orig: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.title_zh: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.
Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”
“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”
The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.
The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.
Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”
The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.
The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.
“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K. , visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.title_zh: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.content_orig:
Bombardier on Friday announced it is expanding in the United State investing $270 million, including $50 million in Wichita  as part of its commitment to growing the site’s capabilities and positioning it for future growth.
The Learning Center represents one component of Bombardier’s broader investment in Wichita. Inaugurated today, the new North American Learning Center reinforces the company’s commitment to developing talent, enhancing capabilities and supporting the long-term growth of its Kansas operations. A ceremony was held on site with Kansas Governor Laura Kelly, Lieutenant Governor David Toland, Bombardier senior leaders and industry stakeholders.
The Learning Center is Bombardier’s first dedicated in-house skills development center for newly hired aircraft technicians and mechanics from across America, helping build the skilled workforce needed to support the company’s growing service and support network, enhancing long-term care and convenience for customers. The program will foster continuous learning and provide employees with a strong foundation for their careers at Bombardier.
The approximately $50 million investment brings together investments in people, infrastructure and capabilities to strengthen the Wichita site for the future. In addition to the new Learning Center, the investment includes the recently expanded Wheel and Tire Shop, which combines state-of-the-art equipment with advanced employee training to expand Bombardier’s Component Repair and Overhaul (CR&O) capabilities, enhancing quality, efficiency and safety.
“Wichita has long been an important part of Bombardier’s story, and we continue to see tremendous opportunity for the site. Our approximately $50 million investment brings together important initiatives across the site, from the new Learning Center to expanded wheel and tire capabilities, strengthening both our people and our operations. This commitment to Wichita’s future will deepen the expertise and capabilities that will allow us to deliver an even stronger experience for our customers, while position the site for continued growth” said Paul Sislian, Executive Vice President, Aircraft Sales and Bombardier Aftermarket Services.
“Since 2019, my administration has partnered with Bombardier to build up the company’s presence in Wichita, which today now includes the new Learning Center, Bombardier Group’s U.S. headquarters, home of Bombardier Defense and the employment of 1,500 Kansans,” said Governor Laura Kelly. “Bombardier’s new $50 million investment underscores the enduring strength of the partnership between Bombardier and Kansas, and one that I expect will continue long into our shared future.”
With ten service and manufacturing facilities across America, including an upcoming service center in Fort Wayne, Indiana,(1) approximately 3,500 employees and a supplier spend of $2.5 billion across America, Bombardier continues to invest in the people, infrastructure and capabilities that support its customers. Wichita remains an important part of that footprint, with recent investments positioning the site to continue evolving alongside Bombardier’s services business and the needs of its customers.

articles.title_zh: Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern
articles.content_orig:
Dwindling academic programmes and official visits risk eroding the next generation of American China specialists
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.
Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.
However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.title_zh: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.content_orig:
New research, facilitated by cutting-edge techniques, led to one of the first examples of physical proof for ancient ritual animal slaughter
Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival.
The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice.
To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial arrangement of valuable artefacts.

articles.title_orig: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.title_zh: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.title_zh: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.content_orig:
How Netanyahu reshaped Israel after 18 years in power
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.
Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.
As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.
Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.
Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.
The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.
In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.
Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.
Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law , which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.
Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.
Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.
A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.
Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.
Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.
Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests : a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.
In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.
But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.
At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.
Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.
But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

Although the findings shed light on how rare earth elements accumulate in carbonatite-related formations, the researchers concluded that the site was unlikely to emerge as a major global alternative to existing producers any time soon.
Lead scientist Professor Yang Xiaoyong noted that the deposit’s mineralisation was “small in scale” and “still far from reaching the large scale of rare earth deposits”. The findings point to the steep geological and economic barriers nations face as they attempt to diversify their sources of critical minerals.

Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon designates China-backed campus cultural centers a threat to US national security
articles.title_zh: Pentagon designates China-backed campus cultural centers a threat to US national security
articles.content_orig:
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth alleges Confucius Institutes operating in disguise on US university campuses
The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.
Hegseth, ‌in a ‌video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius ‌Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
“It turns ‌out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped ​up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds ⁠of American students,” Hegseth said.
The defense department over ​the ​past two months has “systematically ​dismantled every single one of ​these organizations”, he ‌said.
The Chinese ​embassy ​in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.title_zh: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.content_orig:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman warned Friday that the United States is in a "new space race" with China, saying that the agency must recapture the urgency of the Apollo era if it hopes to return astronauts to the moon first.
China launched its first astronaut in 2003, he said, and has since built up a broad portfolio of space capabilities, including lunar missions and plans for a crewed moon landing before 2030. These rapid advances have created a competition far closer than the Cold War race that culminated in the Apollo moon landings, Isaacman said, during an Artemis update at Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida.
"Nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass to our overseas competitors," he said. "The appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion."
NASA reaffirmed its summer plans for Artemis III, and for Artemis IV—the mission scheduled to return astronauts to the lunar surface—in 2028. The agency will continue to depend on Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to achieve these goals.
According to NASA officials, Artemis III will be a two-week mission involving four astronauts and a series of docking demonstrations in Earth's orbit, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing the lunar landers. The mission will not travel to the moon but is designed to test systems and operations needed for future lunar landings.
Artemis III will require multiple launches in quick succession from Florida and give crews an opportunity to conduct docking exercises with both commercial spacecraft, NASA leaders said.
During the briefing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons praised SpaceX's rapid development pace.
"We're seeing lots of hardware, lots of quick changes, and an absolute blistering pace of production," he said.
The agency's push comes as China works toward its publicly stated goal of landing astronauts on the moon before 2030, raising concerns among U.S. officials that America could lose momentum in a domain it once dominated.
Isaacman repeatedly invoked the Apollo era, arguing that NASA should draw lessons from when the agency progressed from Apollo 7's first crewed mission to Apollo 11's lunar landing within nine months.
"It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months," he said.
While emphasizing that NASA will not compromise safety, Isaacman said the agency is working to cut bureaucracy, speed decision-making and increase the pace of hardware development.
The broader goal, he said, extends beyond simply returning astronauts to the moon.
"This will not be a repeat of flags and footprints," Isaacman said.
He described future lunar missions as laying the groundwork for a permanent human presence beyond Earth.
"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon, to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what will begin as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface, " Isaacman said.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.title_zh: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.content_orig:
China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.

articles.title_orig: MTA suspending bus fare enforcement teams after altercations emerge
articles.title_zh: MTA suspending bus fare enforcement teams after altercations emerge
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- The MTA has suspended its Eagle Team fare enforcement unit after a violent encounter in the Bronx came to light, adding to scrutiny surrounding the team's tactics.
The decision came after video showed a man being dragged off a city bus and "practically body slammed" by members of the MTA's Eagle Team after he allegedly threw an elbow and brandished a knife. The incident was described as the latest problematic encounter involving the unit.
Kyle Taylor, who was involved in a separate confrontation with the fare enforcement team, said suspending the unit does not go far enough.
"Is it justification? No. Because the people that did this to me are just suspended. There's nothing happening to them, but yet I'm hurting every night," Taylor said.
Taylor maintains he paid his fare on Oct. 6 when he was stopped in Brooklyn and asked to show proof of payment. He said the confrontation escalated , leaving him unconscious.
"If I would have put my hands on them, I would be in jail. Seven years right?" Taylor said.
The other violent encounter occurred in the Bronx in August. According to MTA leadership, the incident was not reported to the agency at the time, and officials did not learn about it until Thursday. That prompted MTA Chair Janno Lieber to suspend the Eagle Team's field operations.
"I'm not willing to keep our teams active in the field until I know all protocols are being followed," Lieber said.
The Eagle Team's role is to combat fare evasion, which the station's investigative team found cost the city nearly $1 billion last year.
The MTA said it will review the entire operation. If the agency decides to reinstate the Eagle Team, activists say additional accountability measures are needed, including legislation requiring team members to wear body cameras.
"The only thing that the city respects is lawsuit. That's why we filed a $25 million lawsuit," civil rights activist Rev. Kevin McCall said.
Taylor said he plans to continue pursuing his case regardless of whether the Eagle Team returns.
"It's sad in this day and age that I would have to go through this and I paid my fare," he said.

articles.content_orig:
"It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges".
Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume Guérin having a more momentous week.
We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire.
The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and Guérin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable".
What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building.
Guérin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks".
Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president.
"What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says.
For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.
In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.
In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.
Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.
Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.
Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.
It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.
I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?
"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.
Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."
She complains of having to live on €300 per month.
"I feel we are not respected as young adults."
Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.
This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.
In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.
"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."
Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.
"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.
Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.
"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.
Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.
Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.
In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.
With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

articles.content_orig:
Abbas Araqchi, Foreign Minister of the Islamic Republic, stated on Wednesday, October 21, that “the country is truly in a state of war,” adding that hostilities remain ongoing as Iran simultaneously confronts military threats and extensive economic sanctions.
In remarks reported by domestic Iranian media outlets, Araqchi said: “Under current conditions, the country is facing both war and military threats alongside widespread economic sanctions. At present, the reality is that the country is truly in a state of war, and the war is still ongoing.”
In response to a question regarding Tehran’s latest reply to the United States concerning negotiations, the Foreign Minister stated that the Islamic Republic has delivered its proposal to Washington, and the onus now lies on the U.S. to meet Tehran’s conditions.
“Our response is clear,” Araqchi noted. “We have submitted our proposal to the United States. If they are sincere about advancing negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, they must fulfill our conditions for everything to be resolved.”
Reiterating Tehran’s position against American pressure, Araqchi added: “Everyone knows that we will not surrender.”

articles.title_orig: Alleged Chinese agent Wanying Zhang pleads not guilty in Los Angeles courtroom
articles.title_zh: Alleged Chinese agent Wanying Zhang pleads not guilty in Los Angeles courtroom
articles.content_orig:
A Southern California realtor accused of being a Chinese foreign agent pleaded not guilty to the allegations in a Los Angeles federal courtroom Friday.
Wanying Zhang, 34, appeared in a white jumpsuit and shackles, speaking only to deny charges that she surveilled the Taiwanese president's son in a Seattle suburb in September 2025.
The plea puts the case on track for a trial that will require the Justice Department to lay out its evidence of the allegations she conspired with Chinese intelligence officials for what prosecutors called a spy mission.
She was arrested earlier this month at L.A. International Airport while attempting to board a flight to China. She has been charged with one count of acting in the U.S. as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang's husband, Edric Ding, had appeared in earlier court hearings. The couple have been realtors together at the same firm in Irvine, California.
But Ding did not appear at the short hearing on Friday. This is after prosecutors claimed in a recent court filing that Zhang was having an affair with a man who accompanied her on the alleged surveillance mission to Washington state last year. CBS has identified him as Fatai Miao, a construction entrepreneur who recently left Southern California on a one-way ticket to China.
Miao's son told CBS News he does not believe his father was working for the Chinese government, and Miao has not been charged with any crime.
The judge set a pretrial hearing for Nov. 12. The trial is scheduled to begin Nov. 30 at a federal courthouse in Santa Ana, California, and will last an estimated four days.
Both prosecutors and Zhang's attorney, Craig Harbaugh, declined to comment on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Duchess of Sussex was told of ‘disturbing allegations’ against her father in 2018
articles.title_zh: Duchess of Sussex was told of ‘disturbing allegations’ against her father in 2018
articles.content_orig:
The Metropolitan Police says it is investigating reports that a letter was sent to one of its specialist units in 2018 containing allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Meghan released a statement saying that a letter was sent to the force containing "disturbing allegations" about the behaviour of her estranged father, and subsequently shared with her.
On Friday, it was reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle, 82, were found in his former home in the Philippines. The Sun newspaper, which first carried the claims , later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against him.
UK police are not investigating Thomas Markle, who is based in the US and strenuously denies the allegations made against him.
Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago.
According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre.
A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018.
"We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."
Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes.
He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.
In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".
Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.
The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.
Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination.
Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".
The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."
Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.
The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.
At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding.
It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry.
Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation.
Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said.
In her statement released on Friday, Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families".
"I am deeply distressed", she said. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed".
She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children".
The BBC has contacted Thomas Markle for additional comment.

articles.title_orig: Over 4 million tubes of toothpaste have been recalled, including kids brands — here’s what you need to know
articles.title_zh: Over 4 million tubes of toothpaste have been recalled, including kids brands — here’s what you need to know
articles.content_orig:
NBC Selected independently determines what we cover and recommend. When you click on or buy through our links, we earn a commission. Learn more .
More than 4.3 million tubes of fluoride toothpaste — many of them kid-themed , in flavors like bubble gum, strawberry and watermelon — have been voluntarily recalled nationwide after the Food and Drug Administration flagged manufacturing problems at the facility that made them.
The recall covers several brands sold under licensed character names, along with a handful of lesser-known labels, and includes tubes with expiration dates stretching into mid-2028, meaning some of the affected toothpaste could be sitting in your medicine cabinet right now.
No illnesses or injuries have been reported. Still, the FDA says families should check lot numbers and expiration dates to see whether their toothpaste is part of the recall. Below, I break down exactly which products are affected, how to tell if you have one and what to do next.
The FDA announced the recall of more than 4.3 million tubes of fluoride toothpaste distributed nationwide because of current good manufacturing practice deviations. Those are federal standards meant to ensure products are made consistently and safely, so a deviation means the manufacturing process didn’t meet requirements, not necessarily that the toothpaste itself is harmful.
The voluntary recall was initiated on September 10 by Pritam International Private Limited, an India-based manufacturer, and the FDA classified it as Class II recall on October 19. A Class II recall is for products that could cause temporary or medically reversible health problems, where the chance of serious harm is considered unlikely. The FDA notice did not report any illnesses or injuries linked to the recalled toothpaste.
Many of the affected tubes were marketed to kids. The recalled products include toothpaste sold under the Brush Buddies, Crayola, Hot Wheels and My Little Pony brands, in flavors such as bubble gum, strawberry, watermelon, peppermint, sweet mint and cool mint. They were distributed by Ashtel Studios Inc. of Ontario, California, and come in 3.5-ounce and 4-ounce tubes, plus a two-pack of 3.5-ounce tubes.
Affected products carry expiration dates from November 2026 through June 2028, and consumers should check the lot numbers and expiration dates on the FDA’s recall notice to see whether theirs is included.
The FDA’s recall notice doesn’t include specific instructions for consumers, and neither the manufacturer nor the distributor has issued public guidance on returns or refunds. Until they do, the safest move is to stop using the toothpaste immediately and toss it out. Start by checking the brand, lot number and expiration date on your tube against the FDA’s recall notice; if it matches, discard it and switch to a different fluoride toothpaste so your family’s brushing routine isn’t interrupted.
Hang on to your receipt or take a photo of the packaging before tossing it, in case a refund process is announced later. No illnesses or injuries have been reported, but if you or your child used the product and have any concerns, you should contact your dentist or doctor immediately.
The below toothpastes were not recalled and have at least a four-star average rating from thousands of customers.
My kids absolutely love this toothpaste — in fact, it is the only one they will use. The fruity flavor makes brushing less of a chore, while fluoride fights cavities and calcium and silica gently clean teeth. It’s approved by the American Dental Association (ADA), free of artificial colors, flavors, and preservatives, and suitable for children ages 2 and up.
This toothpaste’s bright blue, sparkly color will delight kids. Plus, the fluoride formula fights cavities while staying gentle on enamel, and it carries the ADA Seal of Acceptance . It is suitable for children ages 2 and up, with adult supervision.
If you can’t decide on which hello kids’ flavor your little one will love, grab this variety pack that lets them sample all three and pick a favorite. Each toothpaste comes in a brightly colored tube with an easy flip cap that sits flat when closed, so it stands neatly on the bathroom counter.
If you had one of the adult toothpastes in the recall, Crest Pro-Health Advanced is a reliable replacement from a brand you already know. It’s an antibacterial fluoride toothpaste that fights plaque bacteria and supports healthy gums. It also helps whiten teeth and strengthen enamel.
I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness and lifestyle, among other topics. I have also written about the cyclosporiasis outbreak and the recent recall on eggs .

articles.title_zh: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
articles.content_orig:
The Dow slid on Friday as a sell-off in tech in the prior session shifted to other areas of the market and U.S. oil prices topped $100 a barrel amid rising fears that the U.S.-Iran conflict would flare up again.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to settle at 52,215.16, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.21% to close at 25,955.34.
More defensive stocks came under pressure on Friday, with the consumer staples, utilities and healthcare sectors all lower. Dow component American Express fell more than 3% after announcing it was cutting about 5% of its global workforce , citing the need to "prepare for AI." Caterpillar also edged down about 2%, while Goldman Sachs lost more than 1%, adding pressure to the 30-stock index.
On Thursday, many technology stocks had pulled back as traders assessed the impact of outsized corporate borrowing and rising rates on AI and other tech names. Microsoft ticked higher on Friday. However, chip stocks such as Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices made a stronger move, with gains of nearly 3% and almost 2%, respectively.
"For the last two weeks, investors have been sprinting from tech stocks and data center beneficiary stocks to safe stuff, and eventually, you run out of people willing to do that sprint, and that's what today looks like and feels like," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNBC.
Ellerbroek added that tech companies' earnings have proven strong this season, giving investors a reason to embrace tech stocks and focus less on emotion-based flights to safety.
"Emotion and fear play a really big role," the investor said. But, "we've gotten a few tech companies' [latest quarterly financial reports] and their earnings results have been good."
The 10-year Treasury yield was at around 4.999%, up more than 4 basis points on the day. The benchmark yield had fallen below the key 5% level on Thursday for the first time in a month as investors grew cautious about the massive borrowing that is underway to finance the building of AI data centers.
Oil prices also rose on Friday, further pressuring stocks. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 3.8% to settle at $103.27 per barrel. Brent crude prices rose 3.1% to end the session at $116.72 for the highest settle since April. The gains follow reports that the U.S. and Israel may be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran as part of the regional war that started in late February. Iran has countered that it is prepared to strike back as well.
On the week, the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, and the Nasdaq shed 0.7%. The Dow gained 0.4% in the period.
The three major stock indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1.23%, or 652.82 points, to finish at 52,215.16. The S&P 500 ended down 0.52% at 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 0.21% at 25,955.34.
Shares of discount retailers are lower today after analysts at Wells Fargo warned in a note that rising diesel prices could pressure profits through the second half of the year and into 2027.
With third-quarter diesel prices up about 60% year-over-year, analysts estimate the average hit to operating margin will rise to about 27 basis points from 18 basis points in the second quarter. The drag on earnings per share is expected to more than double to 6.2%.
Dollar Tree and Dollar General are down around 5% in midday trading while Five Below and TJX Companies are both down more than 1% on the day. Wells Fargo says Dollar Tree is the most exposed, historically seeing a larger drag than peers when diesel spikes. They estimate the higher fuel costs will weigh on third-quarter profit by about $25 million, or 50 basis points of margin.
The increased costs could mean additional pressure on retail inflation.
Bank of America raised its price target on ServiceNow to $180, implying roughly 15% upside from Thursday's close.
BofA analyst Tal Liani reiterated his buy rating ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings on October 28, citing growing demand for its artificial intelligence offerings.
"We believe ServiceNow's AI could see broader adoption and incremental spend, which should support durable revenue growth," Liani wrote in a Friday note.
The bank's October CIO survey showed that nearly 36% of respondents expect to allocate more than 10% of their software budgets to AI, while nearly 55% said they were likely or very likely to use ServiceNow for back-office AI applications.
The analyst expects third-quarter subscription revenue to grow nearly 21% year over year as IT, customer service, and security adopt new AI products and automation tools.
Uranium, nuclear and clean energy exchange-traded funds all fell to 52-week lows on Friday, while the largest fossil fuel producers in the nation touched all-time highs.
Global X Uranium ETF and Sprott Uranium Miners ETF both dropped to their lowest levels since June 2025, while the VanEck Uranium and Nuclear ETF was at its lowest since May 2025. Of the stocks inside those ETFs, Centrus Energy , Oklo , NuScale Power , Energy Fuels and BWX Technologies were also at 52-week lows Friday.
Clean energy ETFs saw losses, too. Invesco Solar ETF and Invesco WilderHill Clean Energy ETF were at their lowest since September and August last year, respectively, while individual stocks in the group, such as NextPower , Solv Energy , Rivian Automotive and Fluence Energy , also dropped to 52-week lows.
Meanwhile, ExxonMobil , Chevron and ConocoPhillips all traded at all-time highs on Friday.
— Scott Schnipper, Gina Francolla
In a Friday note to clients, Goldman Sachs posed some key questions about hyperscaler Oracle's AI strategy as pressures mount on the AI trade and investors grow increasingly wary to part with capital.
Analyst Gabriela Borges at Goldman said the conversation around Oracle is centering on monetization in proportion to capital expenditures; the sustainability of demand amid customer concentration; and the company's ability to execute despite political pressures facing the data center buildout.
Borges has a buy rating on the stock and a price target of $206, implying upside of 64.1% compared to a closing price recorded as $125.54.
Among the key risks to the company listed by Goldman are "intense capex investment cycle and financing needs."
"Oracle has outlined a FY27 financing framework supported by roughly $20bn of equity issuance (ATM program, already executed), $20 – 25 bn of customer prepayments ($11 bn as of 1Q), ~$20bn of debt issuance (expected in 2HFY27), with the remainder funded through operating cash flow," Borges wrote.
Stocks outside the AI trade are taking the lead.
The S&P 500 Excluding AI index closed Thursday up 12.4% this year, edging out the S&P 500's roughly 12% gain. The gap has converged largely in October.
The ex-AI index is up about 6.6% in October, while the S&P 500, weighed down by concerns around AI financing, is down roughly 0.4%.
The move suggests some leadership broadening beyond AI-linked mega cap names that have dominated in recent periods. By sector, Energy and Consumer Staples are each up double digits in October while Information Technology and Communication Services lead lower, each down more than 5%.
Morgan Stanley reduced its price target on CoreWeave to $70 from $99 Friday, citing mounting financial pressures the so-called neocloud company is facing. The new target still implies 26% upside from Thursday's close.
Shares of CoreWeave, down 2% on Friday, have sold off over the past week amid investor fears over its massive artificial intelligence-rated debt. Its bond yields have also jumped, while the spread on its credit default swaps — which are insurance against default — has widened to levels generally considered distressed.
Morgan Stanley believes CoreWeave's execution has been solid and said it "remains the speed and scale leader in a crowded neocloud ecosystem."

articles.title_orig: Intermountain announces $150M Horowitz gift for Las Vegas children’s hospital project
articles.title_zh: Intermountain announces $150M Horowitz gift for Las Vegas children’s hospital project
articles.content_orig:
An artist's rendering of the Intermountain Health Felicia and Ben Horowitz Children’s Hospital proposed for southwest Las Vegas. The Horowitz family donated $150 million for the $1 billion project. Photo by:
                    


        
            
                Courtesy photo
Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 | 2:16 p.m.
Editor's note: Este artículo está traducido al español.
Three decades ago, while their child received lifesaving care at Lucile Packard Children’s Hospital Stanford in the Bay Area, Felicia Horowitz saw the Packard name on the hospital walls and told herself that one day she would pay it forward.
Today, she and her husband, Ben Horowitz, did just that, committing $150 million to Nevada’s first stand-alone children’s hospital. Intermountain Health officials say the gift ranks among the largest publicly announced donations ever made to a U.S. children’s hospital.
The facility will be named the Intermountain Health Felicia and Ben Horowitz Children’s Hospital.
The gift fulfills that long-ago promise, Ben Horowitz said. When the couple relocated to Southern Nevada about five years ago, he said, his wife was shocked to learn the state had no specialized pediatric hospital.
The new hospital is meant to fill that long-standing gap.
Las Vegas is the largest metro area in the country without a stand-alone children’s hospital. Nevada ranks 48th in pediatricians per capita, and nearly 30,000 Nevada families leave the state each year to get care for their children.
“I don’t want anyone to go through what (our child) did, but I know they will because that is how the world works,” Ben Horowitz said. “I don’t want anyone in Las Vegas to lose a child because we don’t have the right health care.”
Intermountain said the donation will help create a welcoming, child-centered environment for families, recruit leading pediatric specialists and expand access to specialized care.
Yet when Felicia Horowitz took the stage this afternoon at the hospital’s future site in southwest Las Vegas, she insisted the gratitude was flowing in the wrong direction.
“The whole point of the gift, it’s about (a) thank-you,” she said, before thanking the region’s hospital workers, retail workers and Metro Police.
She then asked the crowd to stand and applaud the city’s healthcare workforce.
“They are truly the heartbeat of the state,” she said.
David Flood, Intermountain Health’s chief development officer, echoed the weight of the moment.
“We are not just building a hospital,” he said. “We are standing on sacred ground. It will be sacred for the families receiving care.”
Ben Horowitz co-founded the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. Felicia Horowitz is CEO of the Horowitz Family Foundation and is active with local organizations including the Cleveland Clinic Lou Ruvo Center for Brain Health, the University Medical Center Foundation and the Las Vegas Raiders Foundation.
The Horowitz donation caps a run of major gifts to the project.
Earlier this month, Larry and Heidi Canarelli, whose family has built homes in Southern Nevada for decades, pledged $50 million. The hospital’s inpatient tower will bear their name.
In August, the Raiders and three team co-owners pledged $25 million: $10 million from the team and $5 million each from owner Mark Davis and limited partners Egon Durban and Michael Meldman. Davis called it the largest philanthropic commitment in franchise history, and the hospital’s bistro and inpatient rehab gym will carry the Raiders name.
Singer Bruno Mars gave $1 million at a public event in April.
The hospital will be built at UNLV’s Harry Reid Research and Technology Park, near Sunset Road and Durango Drive.
Intermountain estimates the project will cost more than $1 billion and has committed to covering two-thirds of it. Clark County commissioners unanimously approved the development and use permits, including one for a heliport, in May.
The inpatient tower is scheduled to open in 2030 with 180 beds and room to expand to 228. Intermountain expects the hospital to create about 1,300 jobs and generate roughly $800 million a year in economic impact for the county.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian negotiator says local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian negotiator says local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump has brokered a coming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can be delivered and civilians can be evacuated from a place she said is “on the brink of disaster.”
The localized ceasefire is set to begin next week.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian relief to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Melania Trump, who worked with officials from both countries on a separate matter, initiated talks about Oleshky after learning about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said in announcing her involvement.
She and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire, the White House said.
Ukraine’s top negotiator in the effort told The Associated Press that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
Russian officials also confirmed the agreement.
Lubinets earlier Friday thanked Melania Trump and said the deal would be tough to accomplish. He said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said.
Lubinets said the operation would involve removing mines on the way to Oleshky before the physical delivery of humanitarian supplies and the arranging of evacuations.
He gave no further details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or implemented, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to comment when asked if Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
“When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination,” he said. “For several weeks, we discussed many questions, initiatives and ideas. We established new approaches, mechanisms and tools to do everything possible to help civilians in Oleshky survive.”
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday in Moscow” — or late Monday in the United States — “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.”
Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on “organizing a humanitarian mission” in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia’s priority.
The first step will be to clarify what people need and organize the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the first lady. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort.
Peskov said “those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether they would be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days.
Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman.
“What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president told reporters at the White House.
Beckman portrayed the first lady’s work on the ceasefire as an extension of her efforts to help reunite Russian and Ukrainian children with their families after they were separated by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions , reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process , Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington, Volodymyr Yurchuk, Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Wolves Descend on Finnish Villages After Google Hacked Down 1,300 Acres of Habitat to Make Room for AI Data Centers
articles.title_zh: Wolves Descend on Finnish Villages After Google Hacked Down 1,300 Acres of Habitat to Make Room for AI Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
Google has spent more than a decade pointing to Finland as proof that a data center can be a good neighbor. Now Finland’s regulators say it moved too fast on the next ones.
The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority issued a notice that requires Google subsidiary Tuike Finland to suspend all environmentally significant preparatory work at sites in Muhos and Kajaani, until required environmental impact assessments are finished. The move follows the clearing of an estimated 250,000 trees at Muhos, according to The Guardian .
The two sites are part of Google’s €13 billion (about $15.1 billion) investment in Finnish AI infrastructure, announced in September and billed by the company as its largest single investment in Europe. Google already operates a data center in the Finnish town of Hamina.
“This is Google’s largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland’s leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure,” Google said in a statement in September regarding its $15.1 billion plan. The company emphasized “what is possible through strong partnerships to create long-term community value and world-class environmental sustainability.”
But Finland disagrees with how the company has handled its data center buildout.
“In the opinion of the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority, extensive preparatory measures have already been taken in the project areas based on the currently available reports, such as the removal of trees, the stripping of topsoil, the construction of construction site roads and storage areas, changes to ditches and culverts, and stormwater arrangements. In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure,” Tommi Muilu, Head of the Environmental Department at the agency, said in a press release .
The suspension doesn’t cover planning, measurements, soil surveys or other work with minor impacts that can be easily reversed, the agency said.
Google did not respond to a request for comment from Fortune .
The pushback is awkward for a government that went out of its way to land the project. “Finland is an attractive destination for investments, and attracting further investment remains a top priority,” Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in Google’s announcement in September. “Google’s decision is a clear testament to our strengths.”
Not every Finn agrees. More than 96,000 people have signed a citizens’ initiative on the government’s kansalaisaloite.fi platform calling for tighter control of data centers, including a “data center fee.” The initiative asks lawmakers to make sure data centers “do not endanger security of supply or negatively affect the price and adequacy of electricity for consumers and other industries,” following the Irish model of regulating grid access. It also calls for a fee so that “society and local communities are compensated for the environmental damage and resource consumption caused by operations.”
That’s a different picture from the one Google has painted in Finland. In 2009, the company bought a former paper mill in Hamina and turned it into a data center that opened in 2011. It’s cooled with seawater from the Gulf of Finland instead of conventional water cooling. Google also sends the site’s waste heat to local homes and businesses, and estimates that heat recovery will cover up to 80% of Hamina’s district heating network’s annual demand. In September, it signed a 22-year deal with Fortum to help extend the life of the Loviisa nuclear plant, which Google says supplies about 10% of Finland’s electricity.
Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.
